RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__Cardiology & VTE:
Three scores dominate the acute coronary syndrome (ACS) pathway, and each answers a different question. HEART risk-stratifies undifferentiated chest pain in the emergency department (ED) to predict short-term major adverse cardiac events (MACE) and guide safe discharge. TIMI predicts the 14-day risk of death, myocardial infarction (MI) or urgent revascularisation in confirmed unstable angina (UA)/NSTEMI. GRACE predicts in-hospital and 6-month mortality after a diagnosed ACS and, in the UK, drives the timing of invasive angiography. Knowing which tool fits which patient is the high-yield point.

1Which score, and where

The scores sit at different points along the pathway — from the front door to the post-diagnosis decision.

HEART — the ED patient with chest pain of unknown cause. Answers: is this safe to send home?
TIMI — the patient with diagnosed UA/NSTEMI. Answers: what is their short-term event risk?
GRACE — the patient with confirmed ACS. Answers: what is their mortality, and how urgently do they need angiography?
2HEART score — ED chest-pain triage (0–10)

Five components, each scored 0, 1 or 2, giving a total of 0–10. The acronym H-E-A-R-T makes it easy to recall.

Slightly (0) / moderately (1) / highly (2) suspicious
📈ECG
Normal (0) / non-specific repolarisation (1) / significant ST deviation (2)
🎂Age
<45 (0) / 45–64 (1) / ≥65 (2)
⚠️Risk factors
0 (0) / 1–2 (1) / ≥3 or known atherosclerosis (2)
🩸Troponin
≤normal (0) / 1–3× normal (1) / >3× normal (2)
0–3 (low)→~1–2% 6-week MACE — consider discharge with safety-netting
4–6 (moderate)→~12–17% MACE — admit / observe, serial troponin & ECG
7–10 (high)→~50–65% MACE — early invasive management

3GRACE score — post-ACS prognosis & angiography timing

GRACE uses continuous physiological and biochemical variables to estimate in-hospital and 6-month mortality after ACS. In the UK it is the NICE-recommended tool for deciding who needs early invasive angiography.

4Putting it together
Front door: use HEART to decide whether undifferentiated chest pain is safe for discharge.
Diagnosis made: use TIMI or GRACE to quantify risk once UA/NSTEMI is confirmed.
Management decision: GRACE guides the timing of coronary angiography — high risk means early invasive (within 24–72h per NICE).
🚩 Risk scores support decision-making but do not replace clinical judgement. A reassuring (low) score in a patient with ongoing chest pain, dynamic ECG changes or haemodynamic instability still warrants senior review — the pain, not the number, is treated. Scores assume the input variables (especially troponin and ECG) are accurate and interpreted correctly.
🎓 The HEART score is specifically validated for ED disposition of undifferentiated chest pain — a low score (0–3) identifies patients with a very low (~1–2%) 6-week MACE risk who can often be safely discharged. Contrast this with TIMI/GRACE, which are validated in patients already diagnosed with ACS, not for triaging undifferentiated pain.

In non-valvular atrial fibrillation (AF), two complementary scores steer antithrombotic decisions: CHA₂DS₂-VASc estimates annual ischaemic stroke / thromboembolism risk to decide whether to anticoagulate, and HAS-BLED estimates 1-year major bleeding risk to flag and correct modifiable bleeding factors. They are used together, not against each other.

1When to use & what they estimate
Apply to patients with non-valvular AF (paroxysmal, persistent or permanent). CHA₂DS₂-VASc predicts annual risk of stroke and systemic embolism and guides the decision to start a DOAC (first-line) or warfarin. HAS-BLED predicts 1-year risk of major bleeding on anticoagulation — its purpose is to identify and address reversible risk factors, not to deny therapy.
2CHA₂DS₂-VASc components (max 9)
🫀C — Congestive HF
HF or LV dysfunction · 1 point
📈H — Hypertension
history of HTN · 1 point
👴A₂ — Age ≥75
2 points
🍬D — Diabetes
diabetes mellitus · 1 point
🧠S₂ — Stroke/TIA
prior stroke, TIA or thromboembolism · 2 points
🩸V — Vascular disease
prior MI, PAD or aortic plaque · 1 point
🎂A — Age 65–74
1 point
♀️Sc — Sex (female)
female sex category · 1 point
3CHA₂DS₂-VASc thresholds & action
0 (men) / 1 (women, sex point only)→low risk — no anticoagulation
1 (men)→consider anticoagulation, weigh bleeding risk & preference
≥2 (men) / ≥3 (women)→offer anticoagulation — DOAC first-line (warfarin if DOAC unsuitable)
4HAS-BLED components & threshold
📈H — Hypertension
uncontrolled SBP >160 mmHg · 1 point
🫘A — Abnormal renal/liver
1 point each (max 2)
🧠S — Stroke
prior stroke · 1 point
🩸B — Bleeding
prior major bleed or predisposition · 1 point
🧪L — Labile INR
unstable/high INR, low TTR (on warfarin) · 1 point
👴E — Elderly
age >65 · 1 point
💊D — Drugs/alcohol
antiplatelets/NSAIDs & alcohol excess · 1 point each (max 2)
HAS-BLED ≥3→high bleeding risk — review, correct modifiable factors, closer follow-up
🚩 A high HAS-BLED score is NOT a reason to withhold or stop anticoagulation. Its role is to identify and correct modifiable risks — control BP, stop unnecessary antiplatelets/NSAIDs, reduce alcohol, improve INR control — while still protecting the patient from stroke.
🎓 In CHA₂DS₂-VASc, female sex is a risk modifier, not an independent risk factor: a woman with the sex point alone (score 1) does not need anticoagulation. This is why the treatment threshold is ≥2 in men but ≥3 in women.

The Modified Duke Criteria are the standard framework for diagnosing infective endocarditis (IE). They combine microbiological, echocardiographic and clinical findings into MAJOR and MINOR criteria, which are then tallied to classify a suspected case as Definite, Possible, or Rejected IE. The criteria bring structure to a diagnosis that no single test can confirm.

1When to use it & what it does
Apply the criteria to any patient with clinically suspected IE — typically fever plus a new murmur, embolic phenomena, or risk factors such as a prosthetic valve or intravenous drug use (IVDU). The two pillars of a MAJOR diagnosis are positive blood cultures and echocardiographic evidence of endocardial involvement, supported by a set of clinical MINOR criteria. The output is a diagnostic category, not a number.
2MAJOR criteria
🧫Positive blood cultures
Typical IE organism from 2 separate cultures (Strep viridans, Strep gallolyticus/bovis, HACEK, Staph aureus, community-acquired enterococci); OR persistently positive cultures; OR single positive for Coxiella burnetii or phase I IgG titre >1:800
🫀Endocardial involvement
Echo evidence — vegetation, abscess, or new dehiscence of a prosthetic valve; OR new valvular regurgitation
3MINOR criteria
🎯Predisposition
Predisposing heart condition (e.g. prosthetic valve, prior IE) or IVDU
🌡️Fever
Temperature ≥38°C
🩸Vascular phenomena
Septic arterial emboli, Janeway lesions, mycotic aneurysm, conjunctival haemorrhage
🛡️Immunologic phenomena
Osler nodes, Roth spots, glomerulonephritis, positive rheumatoid factor
🔬Microbiological evidence
Positive blood culture not meeting a MAJOR criterion, or serologic evidence of active infection consistent with IE
4Making the diagnosis
2 major→Definite IE
1 major + 3 minor→Definite IE
5 minor→Definite IE
1 major + 1 minor→Possible IE
3 minor→Possible IE
Rejected: a firm alternative diagnosis, resolution with ≤4 days of antibiotics, or criteria for possible/definite IE not met.
🚩 Take 3 sets of blood cultures from different venepuncture sites BEFORE starting antibiotics — premature antibiotics sterilise cultures and can downgrade a Definite case. Transoesophageal echo (TOE) is more sensitive than transthoracic (TTE) for vegetations, abscesses and prosthetic valves — a normal TTE does not exclude IE.
🎓 Peripheral signs made simple: Janeway lesions are painless (J = Just a spot, a vascular phenomenon), whereas Osler nodes are painful (O = Ouch/Osler, an immunologic phenomenon).

Suspected pulmonary embolism (PE) is worked up with a chain of scores that do different jobs: Wells estimates pre-test probability to decide between D-dimer and imaging; PERC lets you rule PE out with no test at all in genuinely low-risk patients; and PESI / sPESI are prognostic — used only once PE is confirmed to predict 30-day mortality and steer inpatient vs outpatient care. The first two are diagnostic gatekeepers; the last is a discharge tool. Keeping that distinction straight is the exam's favourite trap.

1Wells (PE) — pre-test probability

The first decision in any suspected PE. NICE recommends the two-level Wells score to stratify patients before choosing a test. It weights clinical features that make PE more or less likely, with the biggest points for signs of DVT and for the clinician's gestalt that PE is the top diagnosis.

🦵Clinical signs of DVT
leg swelling & pain on palpation — 3
🧠PE is #1 diagnosis
or equally likely as alternative — 3
💓HR > 100
tachycardia — 1.5
🛏️Immobilisation / surgery
in previous 4 weeks — 1.5
🔁Previous DVT / PE
documented prior VTE — 1.5
🩸Haemoptysis
coughing blood — 1
🎗️Malignancy
active/treated within 6 months — 1
2Wells thresholds — which test next

The two-level cut-off drives the whole pathway: it tells you whether a D-dimer is worth doing or whether you should go straight to imaging.

Wells ≤ 4→PE unlikely — do D-dimer; if positive proceed to CTPA, if negative PE excluded
Wells > 4→PE likely — arrange CTPA directly (D-dimer not needed). If CTPA delayed, give interim anticoagulation
If CTPA is contraindicated (e.g. renal impairment, contrast allergy, pregnancy) use a V/Q scan instead.
A negative D-dimer in the "unlikely" group safely excludes PE without any imaging.
3PERC — rule out with no test at all

The PE Rule-out Criteria apply only when clinical gestalt is already low probability. If the patient is low-risk and all 8 criteria are negative, the risk of PE is under ~2% and you can rule it out without even a D-dimer — sparing false positives and unnecessary imaging. A single positive criterion means PERC fails and you fall back to the D-dimer/CTPA pathway.

Age < 50
HR < 100
SaO₂ ≥ 95% on room air
No haemoptysis
No oestrogen use (OCP/HRT)
No prior DVT / PE
No unilateral leg swelling
No surgery/trauma needing hospitalisation in last 4 weeks
All 8 negative (in low-risk pt)→PE ruled out — no D-dimer, no imaging
Any 1 positive→PERC fails — proceed to D-dimer / CTPA per Wells
4PESI / sPESI — prognosis once PE is confirmed

Diagnosis over, the question becomes: can this confirmed PE be managed as an outpatient? PESI (and the simplified sPESI) predict 30-day mortality to guide that call. The simplified version scores 1 point each for six variables:

🎂Age > 80
1 point
🎗️Cancer
1 point
🫁Chronic cardiopulmonary disease
1 point
💓HR ≥ 110
1 point
🩺SBP < 100
1 point
🫁SaO₂ < 90%
1 point
sPESI = 0→Low risk (~1% 30-day mortality) — consider outpatient anticoagulation
sPESI ≥ 1→Not low risk — admit for inpatient monitoring
🚩 D-dimer only helps you rule OUT PE in low/intermediate probability — its specificity is poor (raised by infection, malignancy, pregnancy, surgery, age). In a high-probability (Wells > 4) patient a normal D-dimer does not exclude PE, so skip it and go straight to CTPA. Never let a negative D-dimer override strong clinical suspicion.
🎓 In patients over 50, use an age-adjusted D-dimer threshold (age × 10 µg/L, e.g. cut-off 750 for a 75-year-old) to improve specificity and cut needless CTPAs — a high-yield refinement examiners love.

The Wells Score for DVT is a clinical prediction rule that estimates the pre-test probability of deep vein thrombosis in a patient with a symptomatic leg. It stratifies patients into 'DVT likely' or 'DVT unlikely' groups, which NICE uses to decide who needs an urgent proximal leg vein ultrasound versus who can be triaged with a D-dimer. It is a risk-stratification tool, not a diagnostic test.

1When to use it

Apply it to any adult presenting with a suspected first episode of DVT — a unilaterally painful, swollen or tender leg. It quantifies clinical suspicion before any imaging or D-dimer, guiding the NICE two-level diagnostic pathway. It does not apply to suspected pulmonary embolism (a separate Wells PE score exists) and is not validated in pregnancy.

2The components

Each feature scores +1, except the alternative-diagnosis item which scores −2.

🎗️Active cancer
Treatment within 6 months, or palliative · +1
🦵Paralysis / plaster
Paralysis, paresis or recent plaster immobilisation of the leg · +1
🛏️Immobility / surgery
Bedridden ≥3 days, or major surgery within 12 weeks · +1
👉Localised tenderness
Along the distribution of the deep venous system · +1
🦿Whole-leg swelling
Entire leg swollen · +1
📏Calf swelling >3cm
Measured 10cm below tibial tuberosity vs asymptomatic side · +1
💧Pitting oedema
Confined to the symptomatic leg · +1
🕸️Collateral veins
Superficial, non-varicose collateral veins · +1
🔁Previous DVT
Previously documented deep vein thrombosis · +1
➖Alternative diagnosis
An alternative dx at least as likely as DVT · −2
3Scoring & the two-level threshold

Sum the points. NICE collapses the score into a two-level result:

Score ≥2→DVT likely
Score ≤1→DVT unlikely
4The NICE pathway

The two-level result drives investigation:

Likely (≥2)→Proximal leg vein ultrasound within 4 hours
Likely, scan >4h delayed→D-dimer + interim anticoagulation, scan within 24h
Unlikely (≤1)→D-dimer test
Unlikely + D-dimer positive→Proximal leg vein ultrasound
Unlikely + D-dimer negative→DVT excluded — consider alternative cause
A 'likely' patient goes straight to imaging; D-dimer is only used to buy time if the scan is delayed.
An 'unlikely' patient is filtered by D-dimer first; a negative result safely rules out DVT without a scan.
🚩 If ultrasound is negative but the D-dimer is positive and Wells is 'likely', repeat the proximal scan in 6–8 days. An isolated calf (distal) DVT can be missed on the initial proximal scan and may propagate.
🎓 The −2 'alternative diagnosis' item is the swing factor and the most commonly forgotten component. Forgetting to subtract it wrongly pushes a patient into the 'likely' group; actively ask whether cellulitis, a ruptured Baker's cyst, or superficial thrombophlebitis is at least as plausible.

Venous thromboembolism (VTE) — deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE) — is a leading cause of preventable in-hospital death. Every patient admitted to hospital in the UK must have a documented VTE risk assessment, a nationally mandated safety metric. The assessment weighs the patient's risk of clotting against their risk of bleeding to decide whether to offer mechanical prophylaxis (anti-embolism stockings / intermittent pneumatic compression), pharmacological prophylaxis (usually low-molecular-weight heparin, LMWH), or both. The NICE framework guides the decision; the Caprini score is a validated points-based model that stratifies surgical patients into risk bands to fine-tune prophylaxis intensity and duration.

1When & why — the mandated assessment

NICE requires a VTE risk assessment on every hospital admission, reassessed at 24 hours and whenever the clinical picture changes. The core question is a balance:

Thrombosis risk — how likely is this patient to clot if left unprophylaxed?
Bleeding risk — how dangerous would pharmacological prophylaxis be?

If VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk, pharmacological prophylaxis is offered. If bleeding risk dominates, mechanical methods are used instead (or prophylaxis deferred). The Caprini score operationalises the thrombosis side for surgical patients.

2The two sides — VTE risk vs bleeding risk

🩹Thrombocytopenia
platelets < 75 × 10&sup9;/L
3The Caprini score — surgical risk bands

The Caprini Risk Assessment Model assigns weighted points (1, 2, 3 or 5) to individual risk factors — e.g. minor surgery (1), age 61–74 (2), central venous access (2), previous VTE (3), positive thrombophilia (3), stroke < 1 month (5), elective arthroplasty (5). The total stratifies risk and steers prophylaxis:

0 points→Very low risk — early ambulation only
1–2 points→Low risk — mechanical prophylaxis (IPC)
3–4 points→Moderate risk — pharmacological ± mechanical prophylaxis
≥ 5 points→High risk — pharmacological + mechanical; consider extended-duration LMWH
4Acting on the balance — prophylaxis decisions

Once the two sides are weighed, NICE directs the choice:

VTE risk > bleeding risk→Offer pharmacological prophylaxis — LMWH first-line (fondaparinux if LMWH unsuitable, e.g. HIT); UFH if severe renal impairment (eGFR < 15–30)
Bleeding risk > VTE risk→Avoid pharmacological agents — use mechanical prophylaxis (IPC or anti-embolism stockings); reassess when bleeding risk falls
Duration→Usually until sufficiently mobile or discharged; EXTENDED for elective hip replacement (up to 35 days), knee replacement (10–14 days), and abdominal/pelvic cancer surgery (28 days)

Anti-embolism stockings and IPC address the thrombosis risk without adding bleeding risk, making them the fallback when LMWH is contraindicated.

🚩 VTE risk is not a one-off tick-box: reassess at 24 hours and whenever the clinical situation changes. Mechanical prophylaxis (stockings / IPC) is CONTRAINDICATED in peripheral arterial disease, leg ischaemia, recent skin grafts, severe leg oedema and diabetic/neuropathic legs — check pedal pulses and skin before applying. The score supports, but never replaces, clinical judgement.
🎓 VTE is a leading cause of preventable hospital death, so a documented VTE risk assessment on admission is a nationally mandated safety metric in the UK (audited via CQUIN/NICE). High-yield exam facts: LMWH is first-line pharmacological prophylaxis; fondaparinux is the alternative in heparin-induced thrombocytopenia; and extended prophylaxis (up to 35 days) follows elective hip replacement.

QRISK3 is the UK calculator for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease — it estimates a person’s 10-year risk of a first heart attack or stroke. Its single high-yield action is the statin decision: a risk of ≥10% means offering a statin after lifestyle advice.

1What it is & who it is for

Used in adults 25–84 without established CVD to guide primary prevention. It combines many variables — age, sex, ethnicity, postcode/deprivation, smoking, diabetes, BP (and treatment), cholesterol/HDL ratio, BMI, plus conditions that raise risk such as CKD, atrial fibrillation, rheumatoid arthritis, SLE, migraine, severe mental illness and steroid/antipsychotic use.

2Threshold → action
QRISK3 ≥ 10% (10-year risk)→offer atorvastatin 20 mg for primary prevention, after lifestyle optimisation
QRISK3 < 10%→lifestyle advice (diet, exercise, smoking, alcohol); reassess periodically
Also address modifiable risk: BP control, smoking cessation, weight, diabetes. Lipid disorders / atherosclerosis ›
3When NOT to use QRISK3
Established CVD (previous MI, stroke/TIA, PAD, angina) → this is secondary prevention — give a high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80 mg) regardless of any score.
Type 1 diabetes, CKD (eGFR <60 / albuminuria), and familial hypercholesterolaemia → statin-eligible regardless of QRISK3 — do not calculate it to decide.
QRISK3 tends to under-estimate risk in these groups, which is why they bypass it.
🚩 Do not run QRISK3 to “clear” a patient who already qualifies for a statin on other grounds. Established CVD, T1DM, CKD and familial hypercholesterolaemia are statin-eligible independent of the score.
🎓 Exam pearl. The examiner’s line: QRISK3 ≥10% → offer atorvastatin 20 mg (primary prevention). Established CVD → atorvastatin 80 mg (secondary), no score needed.

The NYHA functional classification grades the symptom burden of heart failure from I to IV. It is quick, reproducible, and — because it tracks how limited the patient is — it both estimates prognosis and helps steer the escalation of drug and device therapy.

1The four classes
Class I→no limitation — ordinary activity causes no symptoms
Class II→slight limitation — comfortable at rest, ordinary activity causes breathlessness/fatigue
Class III→marked limitation — symptoms on less-than-ordinary activity
Class IV→symptoms at rest, worse on any activity
2Why the class matters → action
Symptomatic HFrEF (NYHA II–IV, reduced EF) → start and up-titrate the four pillars: ACE-inhibitor/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, and an SGLT2 inhibitor.
Persistent NYHA II–IV with LVEF ≤35% despite optimal therapy → refer for device therapy (CRT and/or ICD).
Worsening class also flags the need to review adherence, fluid status and reversible precipitants. Chronic heart failure ›
🎓 Exam pearl. NYHA is a functional class, not an anatomical one — it can improve with treatment. The jump from class II to III (symptoms on less-than-ordinary exertion) is the commonly tested boundary and a trigger to intensify therapy.
RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__Respiratory & EN:
CURB-65 is a validated severity score for community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) that stratifies 30-day mortality risk and guides the decision on where to treat the patient — home, general ward, or critical care. It is built from five simple clinical and laboratory variables, each worth one point (maximum 5). Its community sibling, CRB-65, drops the urea component so it can be used in primary care where blood results are not available. The score is a decision aid that sits alongside clinical judgement, not a replacement for it.

1When to use it & what it estimates
Apply CURB-65 to any adult with a clinical/radiological diagnosis of CAP to estimate 30-day mortality and inform disposition. Use CURB-65 in hospital (bloods available) and CRB-65 in the community / GP setting (no urea). It predicts risk of death; higher scores also flag those who may need HDU/ICU support. It does not diagnose pneumonia, choose the pathogen, or measure oxygenation — assess SaO₂ and oxygen requirement separately.
2The five components (1 point each)
The mnemonic is the score's own name. CRB-65 uses the same components but omits Urea.
🧠Confusion
New confusion — AMTS ≤8 or new disorientation in person/place/time
🩸Urea
Blood urea >7 mmol/L (omitted in CRB-65)
🫁Respiratory rate
RR ≥30 breaths/min
💉Blood pressure
SBP <90 mmHg or DBP ≤60 mmHg
🎂Age ≥65
Age 65 years or older
3Scoring, mortality & disposition
Add the points (0–5) and map to severity band and management. Mortality rises steeply across the bands.
CURB-65 0–1→Low severity, mortality <3% — consider home / oral antibiotics
CURB-65 2→Moderate severity, mortality ~9% — consider hospital / short-stay admission
CURB-65 3–5→High severity, mortality 15–40% — admit, assess for ICU/HDU
CRB-65 0→Very low risk — manage at home
CRB-65 1–2→Consider hospital referral / assessment
CRB-65 3–4→High risk — urgent hospital admission
4Linking severity to antibiotics
NICE/BTS tie the severity band to empirical antibiotic choice and route.
Low severity (0–1): oral amoxicillin 5 days (a macrolide/doxycycline if penicillin-allergic).
Moderate severity (2): amoxicillin, usually with a macrolide (e.g. clarithromycin) if atypical cover is warranted; oral or IV depending on the patient.
High severity (3–5): dual therapy — co-amoxiclav + a macrolide, often IV — with senior/critical-care review.
🚩 CURB-65 is an adjunct, not a rule. It underweights youth and comorbidity: a young patient with severe pneumonia can score low yet be critically unwell. Always factor in SaO₂ / oxygen requirement, bilateral or multilobar changes, significant comorbidity, and social circumstances (can they cope at home?). Clinical judgement can and should override a reassuring score.
🎓 Remember the setting split: CRB-65 for GP / community (no bloods needed) and CURB-65 in hospital (includes urea). The "65" in both is age ≥65, and the letters spell the components in order.

Light's criteria are a set of laboratory rules that classify a pleural effusion as an exudate or a transudate — the single most useful branch point in working up fluid on the chest X-ray. The distinction matters because it splits the differential in two: transudates arise from a systemic upset of pressures and are managed by treating the underlying disease, whereas exudates signal a problem within the pleura itself (infection, cancer, inflammation) and usually demand further pleural investigation. You need serum and pleural samples of protein and LDH taken at the same time.

1WHEN TO USE IT & WHAT IT DECIDES
Apply Light's criteria to any newly aspirated pleural effusion of unknown cause. Send paired pleural fluid and serum for total protein and LDH (lactate dehydrogenase). The rules do not tell you the diagnosis — they tell you which list of diagnoses to pursue. Transudate = altered hydrostatic/oncotic pressure pushing ultrafiltrate across an intact pleura; exudate = increased capillary permeability or impaired lymphatic drainage from local pleural pathology.
2THE THREE CRITERIA — ANY ONE = EXUDATE
The fluid is an exudate if ANY ONE of the following is met; if none are met it is a transudate.
Pleural protein / serum protein > 0.5→Exudate
Pleural LDH / serum LDH > 0.6→Exudate
Pleural LDH > 0.66 × upper limit of normal serum LDH (i.e. > two-thirds ULN)→Exudate
None of the three met→Transudate — treat the systemic cause
3WHAT EACH RESULT POINTS TO
Once classified, the causes divide cleanly. Transudates are typically bilateral and driven by fluid balance; exudates are often unilateral and reflect local disease.
💧TRANSUDATE
Heart failure (commonest), liver cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, hypoalbuminaemia, peritoneal dialysis, hypothyroidism, Meigs syndrome
🦠EXUDATE
Infection (parapneumonic effusion, empyema, TB), malignancy, pulmonary embolism, pancreatitis, autoimmune (RA, SLE), oesophageal rupture
4PITFALLS & ADJUNCTIVE FLUID TESTS
Light's criteria are highly sensitive but over-call exudates: about a quarter of true transudates in patients on diuretics (e.g. treated heart failure) are mislabelled exudate, because diuresis concentrates the fluid's protein and LDH. If the picture is clinically a transudate but the numbers say exudate, calculate the serum-minus-pleural albumin gradient — a value > 12 g/L supports a transudate. Other useful pleural fluid tests:
pH < 7.2 in a parapneumonic effusion → complicated → needs a chest drain.
Low glucose → empyema, TB, RA, malignancy.
Raised amylase → pancreatitis or oesophageal rupture.
Milky / raised triglycerides → chylothorax (thoracic duct).
🚩 An effusion with pleural fluid pH < 7.2, frank pus, or organisms on Gram stain/culture is a complicated parapneumonic effusion / empyema — it will not resolve with antibiotics alone and requires a chest drain. Do not wait.
🎓 You only need ONE of the three Light's criteria positive to call an effusion an exudate — this deliberately high sensitivity means very few exudates are missed, at the cost of occasionally over-labelling a diuretic-treated transudate (rescue with the albumin gradient > 12 g/L).

Sore throat is usually viral, yet antibiotics are still over-prescribed. Two validated clinical scores — the Centor criteria and FeverPAIN — estimate the probability that a sore throat is caused by group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus (Strep pyogenes), so antibiotics are targeted at those most likely to benefit. Neither confirms infection; they are decision aids that must sit alongside clinical judgement and NICE guidance.

1When to use & what it estimates
Use in an acute sore throat (pharyngitis/tonsillitis) to gauge the likelihood of streptococcal infection and guide whether an antibiotic is warranted. A higher score means a higher probability of strep and a greater potential benefit from antibiotics; a low score supports safe self-care. NICE lists both, but FeverPAIN is the preferred tool. Neither is diagnostic — throat swab/rapid antigen testing is not routinely needed to apply them.
2Centor criteria (1 point each)
🧫Tonsillar exudate
Pus/exudate on the tonsils — 1 point
🩺Tender nodes
Tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy — 1 point
🌡️History of fever
Fever >38°C — 1 point
🚫Absence of cough
No cough (cough suggests viral) — 1 point
Modified (McIsaac) adds age: +1 if 3–14y, 0 if 15–44y, −1 if ≥45y.
Mnemonic: the four features are conveniently C-E-N-T — Cough absent, Exudate, Nodes, Temperature.
3FeverPAIN (NICE preferred, 1 point each)
🌡️Fever (24h)
Fever in the last 24 hours — 1 point
🧫Purulence
Pus on the tonsils — 1 point
⏱️Attend rapidly
First seen within 3 days of onset — 1 point
🔴Inflamed tonsils
Severely inflamed tonsils — 1 point
🚫No cough/coryza
Absence of cough or coryza — 1 point
The name is the mnemonic: Fever, Purulence, Attend rapidly, Inflamed tonsils, No cough/coryza. Maximum score 5.
4Scoring, thresholds & management
FeverPAIN 0–1 (or Centor 0–2)→Strep unlikely (~13–18% for FeverPAIN 0–1) — no antibiotic; self-care advice
FeverPAIN 2–3→Intermediate (~34–40%) — consider a delayed/back-up antibiotic prescription
FeverPAIN 4–5 (or Centor 3–4)→Strep likely (~62–65%) — consider an immediate antibiotic
First-line antibiotic→Phenoxymethylpenicillin (penicillin V) for 5–10 days; clarithromycin (or erythromycin in pregnancy) if penicillin-allergic
Whatever the score, offer analgesia (paracetamol/ibuprofen) and safety-netting — most sore throats settle within a week without antibiotics.
🚩 Before applying any score, exclude red flags: stridor, drooling, trismus or a unilateral bulging swelling with uvular deviation (quinsy/peritonsillar abscess), and severe systemic illness — these need urgent referral, not a score. Never use amoxicillin for undifferentiated tonsillitis: if the cause is glandular fever (EBV), it triggers a florid maculopapular rash.
🎓 FeverPAIN is NICE-preferred over Centor — it was validated in UK primary care and, when combined with a delayed-prescribing strategy, has been shown to reduce antibiotic use. Remember Centor gives 1 point for the absence of cough, and FeverPAIN captures early presentation ('attend rapidly within 3 days') that Centor does not.

When a patient presents with possible pulmonary embolism (PE), a chain of scores decides the test. The two-level Wells score sets the pre-test probability — it tells you whether to do a D-dimer or go straight to imaging. PERC lets you rule PE out with no test at all in a genuinely low-risk patient. The whole point of the score is the action it triggers, not the number itself.

1Two-level Wells (PE) components

Add the weighted points. The biggest points are for signs of DVT and for your clinical gestalt that PE is the top diagnosis.

🦵Clinical signs of DVT
leg swelling & pain on palpation — 3
🧠PE is the #1 diagnosis
or equally likely as an alternative — 3
💓HR > 100
tachycardia — 1.5
🛏️Immobilisation / surgery
in the previous 4 weeks — 1.5
🔁Previous DVT / PE
documented prior VTE — 1.5
🩸Haemoptysis
coughing blood — 1
🎗️Malignancy
active or treated within 6 months — 1
2Thresholds → which test next
Wells ≤ 4 (PE unlikely)→do a D-dimer: if negative PE is excluded; if positive proceed to CTPA
Wells > 4 (PE likely)→arrange CTPA directly (D-dimer not needed); if CTPA is delayed give interim anticoagulation
If CTPA is contraindicated (renal impairment, contrast allergy, pregnancy) use a V/Q scan instead.
In patients >50 use an age-adjusted D-dimer (age × 10 µg/L) to cut needless CTPAs. Pulmonary embolism & DVT ›
3PERC — rule out with no test at all

The PE Rule-out Criteria apply only when clinical gestalt is already low probability. If the patient is low-risk and all 8 are negative, PE risk is <2% and you can stop — no D-dimer, no imaging.

Age < 50
HR < 100
SaO₂ ≥ 95% on air
No haemoptysis
No oestrogen (OCP/HRT)
No prior DVT/PE
No unilateral leg swelling
No surgery/trauma needing admission in last 4 weeks
All 8 negative (low-risk patient)→PE ruled out — no D-dimer, no imaging
Any 1 positive→PERC fails — fall back to the Wells / D-dimer / CTPA pathway
🚩 A negative D-dimer never excludes PE in a high-probability (Wells >4) patient — its specificity is poor (raised by infection, malignancy, pregnancy, surgery, age). Skip it and go straight to CTPA.
🎓 Exam pearl. The trap is mixing up the jobs: Wells and PERC are diagnostic gatekeepers (before you know if there is a PE); prognostic scores like PESI come after PE is confirmed. Wells ≤4 → D-dimer; Wells >4 → CTPA.

Acute asthma is graded by severity because the category is the treatment decision. UK (BTS/SIGN/NICE) grading runs moderate → acute severe → life-threatening → near-fatal. A single life-threatening feature makes the attack life-threatening, however well the patient looks — and a normal or rising CO₂ is an ominous sign of exhaustion, not reassurance.

1Moderate & acute severe
Moderate→PEF 50–75% best/predicted, no features of acute severe — treat and reassess
Acute severe (ANY one)→PEF 33–50%, RR ≥25, HR ≥110, or cannot complete sentences in one breath
2Life-threatening & near-fatal

In a patient with acute severe asthma, any one of the following makes it life-threatening:

🫁PEF < 33%
best or predicted
🫀SpO₂ < 92%
or PaO₂ < 8 kPa
🤫Silent chest
cyanosis or poor respiratory effort
😵Exhaustion / altered GCS
confusion, coma
💓Arrhythmia / hypotension
haemodynamic compromise
🩸Normal PaCO₂ (4.6–6.0)
“normal” CO₂ = tiring — ominous
Near-fatal→raised PaCO₂ and/or needing mechanical ventilation with high inflation pressures
3Management escalates with severity
O₂ to target SpO₂ 94–98%.
Salbutamol nebs (oxygen-driven); back-to-back / continuous if severe.
Add ipratropium nebs in acute severe / life-threatening.
Steroids early — oral prednisolone or IV hydrocortisone.
IV magnesium sulfate in acute severe not responding / life-threatening.
Refer to ITU / anaesthetics for life-threatening or near-fatal (rising CO₂, exhaustion). Asthma ›
🚩 A normal or rising PaCO₂ in acute asthma means the patient is tiring and heading for respiratory failure — it is a life-threatening / near-fatal sign and mandates senior + ITU review, not reassurance.
🎓 Exam pearl. Learn the life-threatening 33/92 anchors: PEF <33%, SpO₂ <92%. Add silent chest, cyanosis, exhaustion, arrhythmia/hypotension and a normal CO₂. Any one, in an acute-severe attack, escalates management to IV magnesium and ITU referral.

The DECAF score predicts in-hospital mortality in a patient admitted with an acute exacerbation of COPD. It uses five routinely available variables and drives the practical decisions: who is low-risk enough for supported early discharge, and who is high-risk and needs escalation planning and a frank ceiling-of-care discussion.

1The five components (0–6)
🚶Dyspnoea (eMRCD)
5a housebound but self-caring = 1; 5b needs help washing/dressing = 2
🩸Eosinopenia
eosinophils < 0.05 × 10ⁿ/L — 1
🫁Consolidation
on chest X-ray — 1
🧪Acidaemia
pH < 7.30 — 1
💓atrial Fibrillation
on ECG / history — 1
2Bands → what to do
DECAF 0–1→low mortality — suitable for supported / early discharge pathways
DECAF 2→intermediate risk — admit, active inpatient treatment
DECAF 3–6→high mortality — escalate, senior review, and discuss ceiling of care / ITU & NIV suitability
Acute exacerbation with a respiratory acidosis (pH < 7.35 with hypercapnia) despite initial therapy → NIV. COPD ›
🎓 Exam pearl. DECAF spells its own components: Dyspnoea, Eosinopenia, Consolidation, Acidaemia, Fibrillation. A high score is a prompt to plan escalation and ceiling of care early, not just to predict a statistic.

The STOP-BANG questionnaire screens for obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA). It is not diagnostic — its job is to risk-stratify who should be referred for a sleep study, the test that actually confirms OSA and grades its severity.

1The eight yes/no items (1 point each)
😴S — Snoring
loud snoring
🥱T — Tiredness
daytime sleepiness
👀O — Observed apnoea
witnessed stopping breathing
🩺P — Pressure
treated hypertension
⚖️B — BMI
> 35 kg/m²
🎂A — Age
> 50 years
📏N — Neck
circumference > 40 cm
♂️G — Gender
male
2Bands → action
0–2→low risk of OSA
3–4→intermediate risk
5–8→high risk — refer for a sleep study
≥3 → refer for a sleep study (home oximetry / polysomnography) to confirm and grade OSA.
Confirmed moderate–severe OSA → CPAP, plus weight loss, avoid alcohol/sedatives, and DVLA advice if excessive sleepiness. Obstructive sleep apnoea ›
🎓 Exam pearl. STOP-BANG is a screen, not a diagnosis: a score ≥3 earns a sleep study, and it is the sleep study — not the questionnaire — that dictates CPAP. Always give the driving/DVLA advice.

The Ann Arbor staging system (with the modern Lugano modification) describes the anatomical extent of both Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma, while the International Prognostic Index (IPI) stratifies survival in aggressive NHL (classically DLBCL). Staging drives treatment intent and radiotherapy fields; the IPI predicts overall survival and guides intensity of therapy. Together they answer two questions: how far has it spread? and how well is this patient likely to do?

1Ann Arbor / Lugano staging — the four stages

Applied after diagnostic biopsy and staging imaging (contrast CT and PET-CT; bone marrow biopsy where indicated). Stage is defined by the number and distribution of involved nodal regions relative to the diaphragm, plus any extralymphatic (extranodal) spread.

1️⃣Stage I
One lymph node region, OR a single extralymphatic site (IE)
2️⃣Stage II
≥2 nodal regions on the SAME side of the diaphragm
3️⃣Stage III
Nodal regions on BOTH sides of the diaphragm
4️⃣Stage IV
Disseminated / multifocal extralymphatic involvement (bone marrow, liver, lung)

The Lugano classification refines this with PET-CT for staging and response assessment, and pragmatically splits disease into limited (I–II) and advanced (III–IV) for treatment planning.

2The suffixes — A/B, E and S

Each stage carries modifiers that materially change prognosis and management.

A — no B symptoms.
B — B symptoms present: fever >38°C, drenching night sweats, or unintentional weight loss >10% of body weight over 6 months.
E — localised, contiguous extranodal extension from a nodal site.
S — splenic involvement.
Suffix A→Better prognosis; e.g. Stage IIA
Suffix B→Worse prognosis, often intensifies therapy; e.g. Stage IIIB
3IPI for aggressive NHL — the 5 adverse factors (APLES)

The IPI applies to aggressive NHL, classically DLBCL. One point for each of five adverse factors present at diagnosis — mnemonic APLES.

🎂A — Age
Age >60 years (+1)
🚶P — Performance
ECOG performance status ≥2 (+1)
🧪L — LDH
Serum LDH raised (above normal) (+1)
📊E — Extranodal
>1 extranodal site (+1)
🩻S — Stage
Ann Arbor Stage III or IV (advanced) (+1)
4IPI risk bands & related indices

The total (0–5) maps to four risk groups predicting overall survival.

Score 0–1→Low risk — best OS
Score 2→Low-intermediate risk
Score 3→High-intermediate risk
Score 4–5→High risk — poorest OS
R-IPI (Revised IPI) — recalibrated for patients treated with rituximab-containing chemo (R-CHOP), giving three groups: very good (0), good (1–2), poor (3–5).
FLIPI — the Follicular Lymphoma IPI, a distinct index for indolent follicular lymphoma (factors include age, stage, haemoglobin, LDH, number of nodal areas).
🚩 Always specifically ask about B symptoms — fever, drenching night sweats and >10% weight loss. They upgrade the staging suffix (A→B), significantly worsen prognosis, and can change treatment intensity. Do not rely on the patient volunteering them.
🎓 Two mnemonics: B symptoms = the classic triad fever, night sweats, weight loss (“the three that make it B”). IPI factors = APLES — Age >60, Performance status ≥2, LDH raised, Extranodal sites >1, Stage III/IV.

The CRAB criteria define the end-organ damage that separates symptomatic multiple myeloma requiring treatment from asymptomatic plasma cell disorders (MGUS and smouldering myeloma). CRAB is an acronym for the four classic myeloma-defining events attributable to the clonal plasma cell burden: hyperCalcaemia, Renal impairment, Anaemia and Bone lesions. The IMWG update added three biomarkers (SLiM) that now also mandate treatment even before end-organ damage appears.

1When to use it & what it decides
CRAB is applied whenever a clonal plasma cell disorder is confirmed, to decide whether the patient has active myeloma needing therapy rather than a precursor state that is monitored. A myeloma diagnosis requires clonal bone marrow plasma cells ≥10% (or a biopsy-proven plasmacytoma) PLUS ≥1 myeloma-defining event — either a CRAB feature or a SLiM biomarker. Any damage counted must be attributable to the plasma cell disorder, not another cause.
2The CRAB components (end-organ damage)
🦴C — hyperCalcaemia
Corrected calcium >2.75 mmol/L, or >0.25 mmol/L above the upper limit of normal.
🫘R — Renal impairment
Creatinine >177 µmol/L, or eGFR <40 mL/min — often from cast nephropathy (light chains).
🩸A — Anaemia
Haemoglobin <100 g/L, or >20 g/L below the lower limit of normal.
🩻B — Bone lesions
≥1 osteolytic lesion (≥5 mm) on X-ray, CT or PET-CT. Osteoporosis or a vertebral compression fracture without a lytic lesion does not count.
3SLiM biomarkers (IMWG update)
These three biomarkers carry an ~80% risk of progression to CRAB within 2 years, so their presence alone now defines myeloma requiring treatment — allowing therapy before irreversible organ damage occurs.
S — Sixty: clonal bone marrow plasma cells ≥60%.
Li — Light chains: involved:uninvolved serum free light chain ratio ≥100 (involved level ≥100 mg/L).
M — MRI: >1 focal lesion on MRI (each ≥5 mm).
4Putting it together — the diagnostic threshold
Clonal marrow plasma cells <10%, no CRAB, no SLiM, M-protein <30 g/L→MGUS — monitor, no treatment
Plasma cells 10–60% and/or M-protein ≥30 g/L, but NO CRAB and NO SLiM→Smouldering (asymptomatic) myeloma — surveillance
Plasma cells ≥10% (or plasmacytoma) PLUS ≥1 CRAB or SLiM event→Active multiple myeloma — treat
🚩 Hypercalcaemia and acute kidney injury are oncological emergencies, and myeloma is a common underlying cause — treat aggressively with IV fluids. Beware spinal cord compression: new or progressive back pain, leg weakness or bladder/bowel disturbance in a myeloma patient warrants urgent MRI whole spine and dexamethasone.
🎓 Investigations: serum & urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation (paraprotein / Bence Jones protein) plus serum free light chains, and whole-body MRI or low-dose CT for bone disease — the plain skeletal survey is now superseded as it is far less sensitive. Remember the mnemonic CRAB for the end-organ damage and SLiM for the newer biomarkers.

The ISTH DIC score (International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis) is a simple, widely-validated scoring system used to confirm overt disseminated intravascular coagulation. It is applied only when the patient has an underlying condition known to be associated with DIC, and combines four routine coagulation labs into a single score that separates overt (decompensated) DIC from non-overt (early / compensated) disease.

1WHEN TO USE IT & THE PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

The score is only valid as an entry criterion when a recognised precipitant is present. Do not apply it to a patient with no DIC-associated illness.

Sepsis — the commonest trigger, especially Gram-negative
Malignancy — solid tumours & acute promyelocytic leukaemia
Obstetric emergencies — placental abruption, amniotic fluid embolism, retained products, pre-eclampsia/HELLP
Major trauma, burns, severe pancreatitis & transfusion/haemolytic reactions

Mechanism: a systemic insult drives widespread activation of coagulation. Diffuse thrombin generation deposits microthrombi in small vessels (causing organ ischaemia) while simultaneously consuming platelets and clotting factors faster than they can be replaced. The result is the paradox of DIC — thrombosis and bleeding at the same time — with secondary fibrinolysis raising D-dimer/FDP.

2THE FOUR LAB COMPONENTS & THEIR POINTS

Each variable is banded and scored; the four scores are summed (range 0–8).

🩸PLATELET COUNT
>100 ×10⁹/L = 0 · 50–100 = 1 · <50 = 2
🧪FIBRIN MARKER (D-DIMER / FDP)
No rise = 0 · moderate rise = 2 · strong rise = 3
⏱️PROLONGED PT
<3 s = 0 · 3–6 s = 1 · >6 s = 2
🧬FIBRINOGEN
>1 g/L = 0 · <1 g/L = 1

The elevated fibrin marker (D-dimer or FDP) carries the most weight, reflecting the intense fibrin turnover that defines DIC.

3SCORING, THRESHOLD & ACTION
Score ≥ 5→Compatible with OVERT DIC — repeat the score DAILY to track trajectory
Score < 5→Suggestive of NON-OVERT DIC — repeat scoring in 1–2 days

The score is a diagnostic confirmation, not a treatment threshold. A rising score over serial days signals decompensation; a falling score suggests the coagulopathy is resolving as the trigger is controlled.

4CLINICAL USE & DYNAMIC INTERPRETATION

DIC is a clinicopathological diagnosis — the score supports, but does not replace, the clinical picture. Its greatest value is in serial testing: watch the trend, not a single number. Isolated abnormalities may reflect the underlying illness (e.g. liver disease also raises PT and lowers fibrinogen), so interpret in context.

A falling platelet count and falling fibrinogen across serial samples is a powerful dynamic clue — more informative than any single value
A single normal fibrinogen can mislead early: it is an acute-phase reactant and may start high before it falls
🚩 DIC is ALWAYS a SECONDARY phenomenon — the cornerstone of management is treating the underlying cause (source control in sepsis, delivery in obstetric DIC, etc.). Blood-product support — platelets, FFP, and cryoprecipitate/fibrinogen concentrate for low fibrinogen — is given only if the patient is bleeding or at high bleeding risk (e.g. pre-procedure), NOT to correct numbers alone. A steadily falling fibrinogen with falling platelets on serial tests is a key warning of worsening consumption.
🎓 Learn the classic overt DIC lab picture as one gestalt: low platelets, low fibrinogen, prolonged PT/APTT, raised D-dimer, plus schistocytes (red-cell fragments) on the blood film. That combination in a septic, obstetric, or trauma patient is DIC until proven otherwise.

The 4T score is a bedside pre-test probability tool for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT). It scores four features — Thrombocytopenia, Timing of the platelet fall, Thrombosis, and oTher causes — each 0, 1 or 2 (max 8). It answers a single practical question: is HIT likely enough to stop heparin and send confirmatory testing? HIT is not a simple drug-induced low platelet count — IgG antibodies against platelet factor 4 (PF4)–heparin complexes activate platelets, producing a paradoxical PROTHROMBOTIC state with thrombosis despite falling platelets.

1When to use it & what it estimates
Apply the 4T score to any patient who develops thrombocytopenia (or a significant platelet fall) while on, or recently exposed to, any form of heparin — unfractionated, LMWH, even line flushes. It estimates the pre-test probability of HIT and stratifies patients into low / intermediate / high probability, directing whether to stop heparin, switch anticoagulant, and send anti-PF4 antibody testing. It is a triage tool, not a diagnosis.
2The four Ts (score each 0–2)
📉Thrombocytopenia
Magnitude of platelet fall. 2 = >50% fall AND nadir ≥20; 1 = 30–50% fall or nadir 10–19; 0 = <30% fall or nadir <10 (×10⁹/L).
⏱️Timing
2 = clear onset day 5–10 (or ≤1 day if heparin within past 30 days); 1 = consistent but unclear, or after day 10; 0 = <4 days without recent exposure.
🩸Thrombosis
2 = new confirmed thrombosis, skin necrosis, or acute systemic reaction after IV heparin bolus; 1 = progressive/recurrent or suspected thrombosis; 0 = none.
🔍oTher cause
Other explanation for the low platelets. 2 = none apparent; 1 = possible; 0 = definite alternative cause (sepsis, drugs, DIC).
3Scoring bands & action
0–3 (low)→HIT unlikely (~<5%). High negative predictive value — HIT effectively ruled out; usually no antibody testing needed.
4–5 (intermediate)→Stop heparin, start a non-heparin anticoagulant, send anti-PF4 testing.
6–8 (high)→HIT probable — act as above urgently; treat as HIT until confirmatory testing returns.
4Management if intermediate / high probability
STOP all heparin — including flushes and LMWH.
Start a non-heparin anticoagulant: argatroban, danaparoid, or fondaparinux.
Send HIT antibody (anti-PF4) ELISA ± a functional assay (e.g. serotonin release assay) to confirm.
Do NOT transfuse platelets — this fuels thrombosis.
Avoid warfarin until platelets recover — risk of venous limb gangrene / skin necrosis.
🚩 HIT causes THROMBOSIS, not bleeding — never give platelet transfusions, as they fuel clotting. A low 4T score (0–3) has a high negative predictive value and reliably rules HIT out.
🎓 Timing of 5–10 days is classic — think HIT whenever platelets drop about a week into heparin therapy. Confirm with anti-PF4 antibodies, but act on the 4T score first.

The FIGO staging system (Fédération Internationale de Gynécologie et d'Obstétrique) is the internationally adopted anatomical staging framework for gynaecological malignancies. It describes how far a cancer has spread from its organ of origin, and this stage is the single strongest driver of both prognosis and management. FIGO uses a unified logic across all sites — Stage I confined to the organ of origin, Stage II local/pelvic spread, Stage III regional/nodal or wider pelvic/abdominal spread, and Stage IV distant metastasis or invasion of bladder/bowel mucosa — but the modality of staging differs by cancer.

1THE UNIFYING I→IV PRINCIPLE

Every FIGO stage, whatever the organ, follows the same escalating anatomical journey: organ → local → regional → distant. Learn this backbone once and the organ-specific detail hangs off it.

STAGE I→Confined to the organ of origin (cervix / uterus / ovary)
STAGE II→Local spread beyond the organ but still within the pelvis
STAGE III→Regional spread — pelvic sidewall, lower vagina, peritoneum outside pelvis, or lymph nodes (pelvic/para-aortic)
STAGE IV→Distant metastasis, or invasion of bladder / bowel mucosa, or spread beyond the abdomino-pelvic cavity
2STAGING MODALITY — HOW EACH IS STAGED

A high-yield distinction: the method of assigning stage is not the same across the three main cancers.

Cervical — classically CLINICAL (examination, colposcopy, EUA). The current FIGO revision now permits imaging and pathology (MRI, CT/PET, surgical nodal findings) to assign stage — nodal disease became stage IIIC.
Endometrial — SURGICALLY (pathologically) staged at total hysterectomy + bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy ± nodal assessment.
Ovarian — SURGICALLY staged at laparotomy with peritoneal washings, omentectomy, biopsies and nodal sampling.
3CERVICAL CANCER — FIGO STAGING

Historically staged clinically; the current FIGO revision now incorporates imaging and pathology.

🔵STAGE I
Confined to the cervix (IA microscopic/measured; IB clinically visible or larger)
🟢STAGE II
Beyond uterus but NOT to pelvic wall or lower third of vagina (IIA upper vagina; IIB parametrium)
🟠STAGE III
Pelvic wall / lower third vagina / hydronephrosis or non-functioning kidney; IIIC = pelvic (IIIC1) or para-aortic (IIIC2) nodes
🔴STAGE IV
IVA — bladder/rectal mucosa or beyond true pelvis; IVB — distant metastasis
4ENDOMETRIAL CANCER — SURGICALLY STAGED

Staged pathologically; myometrial invasion depth defines the split within stage I.

🔵STAGE I
Confined to uterine body — IA <50% myometrial invasion; IB ≥50% invasion
🟢STAGE II
Invades cervical stroma but not beyond the uterus
🟠STAGE III
Local/regional spread — serosa/adnexa (IIIA), vagina/parametrium (IIIB), pelvic or para-aortic nodes (IIIC)
🔴STAGE IV
IVA — bladder/bowel mucosa; IVB — distant metastasis (including intra-abdominal / inguinal nodes)
5OVARIAN CANCER — SURGICALLY STAGED

Staged at laparotomy; often diagnosed late because early disease is silent.

🔵STAGE I
Limited to the ovaries — IA one ovary, capsule intact; IB both ovaries; IC capsule breach / surface tumour / positive washings
🟢STAGE II
Extension to other pelvic organs (uterus, tubes, or other pelvic tissue) below the pelvic brim
🟠STAGE III
Peritoneal spread outside the pelvis and/or retroperitoneal (pelvic/para-aortic) lymph nodes
🔴STAGE IV
Distant metastasis — pleural effusion with positive cytology (IVA), or liver/splenic parenchymal or extra-abdominal spread (IVB)
🚩 Stage drives both management and prognosis at every site. Ovarian cancer typically presents late (stage III/IV) because symptoms are vague and non-specific — persistent bloating, early satiety, abdominal distension, pelvic/abdominal pain and urinary urgency. Maintain a high index of suspicion in women (especially ≥50), and investigate with CA-125 and pelvic ultrasound as per NICE. Do not wait for an obvious mass.
🎓 Remember the single unifying rule: organ → local → regional → distant maps onto Stage I → II → III → IV for every gynae cancer. For modality, the exam hook is: endometrial and ovarian are SURGICALLY staged, whereas cervical was classically CLINICAL (the current FIGO revision now folds in imaging/pathology, making nodal disease stage IIIC).

The MASCC risk index (Multinational Association for Supportive Care in Cancer) risk-stratifies an episode of febrile neutropenia into low or high risk, to decide whether a patient can step down to oral / outpatient antibiotics or needs inpatient IV therapy. Crucially it is a de-escalation tool used after the emergency has been treated — neutropenic sepsis kills, and empirical antibiotics come first.

🚩 Neutropenic sepsis is an emergency. In any patient on chemotherapy (usually within ~7–14 days) with temperature ≥38°C (or unwell) and neutrophils <0.5 (or <1.0 and falling), give empirical IV broad-spectrum antibiotics — piperacillin-tazobactam — within 1 hour ("door-to-needle"), after cultures but without waiting for the count. Do not calculate MASCC first.
1MASCC components (higher score = lower risk; max 26)
🌡️Burden of illness
no/mild symptoms +5; moderate +3 (severe 0)
🩸No hypotension
SBP ≥90 mmHg — +5
🫁No COPD
+4
🧬Solid tumour / no prior fungal infection
+4
💧No dehydration
not needing parenteral fluids — +3
🏠Outpatient at fever onset
+3
🎂Age < 60
+2
2Threshold → oral/outpatient vs inpatient IV
MASCC ≥ 21 (low risk)→once stable and responding, consider early switch to oral antibiotics (co-amoxiclav + ciprofloxacin) and outpatient management with clear safety-netting
MASCC < 21 (high risk)→admit and continue IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam), inpatient monitoring
MASCC steers where and how to treat — it never delays the first dose. Neutropenic sepsis ›
🎓 Exam pearl. Two-step logic: treat first (piptaz within 1 hour, don’t wait for the count), then risk-stratify with MASCC — ≥21 low risk may go to oral/outpatient, <21 high risk stays on IV as an inpatient.
RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__GI — Bleeding &:
Acute upper GI bleeding is risk-stratified with two complementary scores. The Glasgow-Blatchford Score (GBS) is a pre-endoscopy tool using only clinical parameters and bloods to identify low-risk patients who may avoid admission or intervention. The Rockall score predicts rebleeding and mortality: a pre-endoscopy (clinical) version exists, but the full/complete Rockall requires endoscopic findings. In short — GBS answers \"can this patient go home?\", Rockall answers \"how likely are they to rebleed or die?\".

1WHEN TO USE EACH SCORE

NICE recommends the GBS at first assessment of anyone with acute upper GI bleed, and the full Rockall score after endoscopy.

GBS — front-door triage. Purely clinical + bloods, no endoscopy needed. Estimates the risk of needing intervention (transfusion, endoscopic therapy, surgery) or death, and flags who can be managed as an outpatient.
Pre-endoscopy (clinical) Rockall — age, shock and comorbidity only; a quick early estimate of risk.
Full/complete Rockall — adds endoscopic diagnosis and stigmata of recent haemorrhage; predicts rebleeding and mortality after the scope.
2GLASGOW-BLATCHFORD COMPONENTS

Points are assigned from admission bloods and observations. No endoscopy, no age term.

🧪BLOOD UREA
Rising urea scores 2–6 points (higher urea = more points)
🩸HAEMOGLOBIN
Sex-specific thresholds; lower Hb scores 1–6 points
📉SYSTOLIC BP
Lower systolic BP scores 1–3 points
💓PULSE ≥100
Tachycardia scores 1 point
⚫MELAENA
Presentation with melaena scores 1 point
😵SYNCOPE
Presentation with syncope scores 2 points
🫘HEPATIC DISEASE
Known liver disease scores 2 points
🫀CARDIAC FAILURE
Known cardiac failure scores 2 points
3GBS SCORING & THRESHOLDS

The GBS ranges from 0 to 23. It rises with the severity of the bleed and the need for intervention.

GBS = 0 (some centres ≤1)→Very low risk — consider outpatient management / discharge with early clinic review; intervention very unlikely
GBS ≥1→Admit — increasing risk of needing transfusion, endoscopic therapy or surgery
GBS ≥7 (approx.)→High risk — high likelihood of requiring endoscopic intervention
4ROCKALL — REBLEEDING & MORTALITY

Rockall scores each variable, with the full score maxing at 11. Higher scores predict higher mortality and rebleeding risk.

Clinical (pre-endoscopy) variables: age, shock (pulse ≥100 and/or systolic BP <100), and comorbidity.
Endoscopic variables (added for full score): the diagnosis (e.g. Mallory-Weiss vs malignancy) and stigmata of recent haemorrhage (e.g. active bleeding, visible vessel, adherent clot).
Full Rockall = 0–2→Low risk of rebleeding and death — good prognosis
Full Rockall ≥3→Increasing risk — mortality climbs steeply with higher scores
5Drug adjuncts you must state
Suspected variceal bleed→terlipressin + prophylactic antibiotics (e.g. IV ceftriaxone) at presentation, before endoscopy → endoscopic band ligation
Non-variceal (peptic ulcer)→endoscopic haemostasis for high-risk stigmata, then a PPI (PPIs are given after endoscopic therapy, not routinely before) — treat H. pylori
Resuscitation and the risk scores come first; these drugs are the "what to do next" once a source is suspected. Acute GI bleed ›
🚩 Resuscitate first — scores never come before the patient. Manage acute upper GI bleeds with an ABCDE approach: transfuse, correct coagulopathy, and activate the major haemorrhage protocol if needed. A risk score must never delay resuscitation or endoscopy in an unstable patient. Endoscopy should be within 24 hours (immediately after resuscitation if an unstable variceal bleed is suspected).
🎓 The GBS uses NO endoscopy — it is purely clinical and biochemical, making it ideal at the front door. A raised urea out of proportion to creatinine is a classic clue to an upper GI bleed: digested blood in the gut is absorbed as a protein meal, driving urea up while renal function stays normal.

The Rockall score risk-stratifies patients with acute upper GI bleeding (UGIB) for rebleeding and mortality. The full (complete) Rockall is calculated after endoscopy and combines clinical variables with endoscopic findings; it runs 0–11. A pre-endoscopy (clinical) Rockall uses only the first three components (age, shock, comorbidity; max 7) for early triage.

1WHEN TO USE IT
Apply the full Rockall after diagnostic endoscopy in a patient with confirmed acute UGIB to estimate the risk of rebleeding and death. Resuscitation (ABC, IV access, fluids/blood) always comes first—scoring never delays management. The pre-endoscopy portion can be scored at the bedside on admission; the endoscopic portion completes the score once the bleeding source is seen.
2THE FIVE COMPONENTS (0–11)
🎂AGE
<60 = 0 · 60–79 = 1 · ≥80 = 2
🩺SHOCK
No shock (pulse <100, SBP ≥100) = 0 · Tachycardia (pulse ≥100, SBP ≥100) = 1 · Hypotension (SBP <100) = 2
🫀COMORBIDITY
None = 0 · Cardiac failure / IHD / major comorbidity = 2 · Renal failure, liver failure, metastatic cancer = 3
🔬DIAGNOSIS
Mallory-Weiss tear / no lesion / no stigmata = 0 · All other diagnoses = 1 · Upper GI malignancy = 2
🩸STIGMATA (SRH)
None or dark spot = 0 · Blood in upper GI tract, adherent clot, visible or spurting vessel = 2
Pre-endoscopy (clinical) Rockall = age + shock + comorbidity only (max 7).
Full (complete) Rockall adds diagnosis + stigmata of recent haemorrhage (max 11).
3SCORING & THRESHOLDS
Score < 3→Good prognosis · low rebleed & mortality risk · consider early discharge
Score 3–7→Intermediate risk · inpatient observation, risk rising with score
Score ≥ 8→High risk · predicts high mortality · escalate / critical-care input
4INTERPRETATION & CLINICAL USE
A higher score means greater risk of both rebleeding and death. High-risk endoscopic stigmata of recent haemorrhage (active spurting/oozing, non-bleeding visible vessel, adherent clot) drive the endoscopic points and identify lesions needing endoscopic haemostasis. These endoscopic appearances map onto the Forrest classification: Forrest I (active bleeding) and IIa (visible vessel) carry the highest rebleeding risk. Contrast the full Rockall with the Glasgow-Blatchford score (GBS), a purely pre-endoscopy tool using clinical and lab data (urea, Hb, SBP, pulse, melaena, syncope, hepatic/cardiac disease) to predict the need for intervention (transfusion, endoscopic therapy, surgery); a GBS of 0 may allow safe outpatient management.
🚩 The full Rockall requires endoscopy findings—do not confuse it with the Glasgow-Blatchford score (pre-endoscopy triage for intervention need). Resuscitation always precedes scoring. Remember the Forrest classification describes the endoscopic stigmata: Forrest I (active bleeding) predicts the highest rebleeding risk.
🎓 High-risk stigmata—active bleeding and a non-bleeding visible vessel—warrant endoscopic haemostasis and independently predict rebleeding. A pre-endoscopy Rockall of 0 or a full Rockall < 3 flags low-risk patients suitable for early discharge.

The Oakland score is a validated risk-stratification tool for acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding (LGIB). It combines seven clinical and laboratory variables into a total of up to ~35 points, identifying low-risk patients who can be safely managed as outpatients rather than admitted. Most lower GI bleeds are self-limiting, and the score gives an evidence-based, NICE-endorsed way to avoid unnecessary admission while flagging those who need inpatient care.

1When to use it & what it predicts
Apply the Oakland score to adults presenting with acute lower GI bleeding (fresh PR bleeding / haematochezia) once initial assessment and resuscitation have been performed. It predicts the probability of a safe discharge — i.e. the absence of an adverse outcome, defined as rebleeding, need for red-cell transfusion, therapeutic intervention (endoscopic, radiological or surgical) or death. A low score identifies patients with a >95% probability of no adverse outcome. Remember most LGIB is self-limiting, with diverticular disease and angiodysplasia the commonest causes.
2The seven components
📅Age
rising points with older age (0–2)
♂️Sex (male)
male +1
🏥Previous LGIB admission
prior admission with lower GI bleed +1
🩸DRE findings
blood on rectal examination +1
💗Heart rate
rising points with tachycardia (0–3)
🩺Systolic BP
rising points with lower SBP (0–5)
🧪Haemoglobin
biggest weighting — lower Hb scores heavily (up to ~22)
Haemoglobin dominates the score — a low Hb alone can push a patient well above the discharge threshold.
The three admission/history items (male, prior LGIB, blood on DRE) each add just 1 point.
3Scoring & thresholds
Score ≤ 8→>95% probability of safe discharge — consider outpatient management
Score > 8→Higher risk of adverse outcome — admit for inpatient assessment
A ≤8 cut-off is the NICE-endorsed threshold for safe outpatient discharge in stable patients.
The higher the score, the greater the risk of rebleeding, transfusion, intervention or death.
4Interpretation & clinical use
Use the score to guide disposition, not to override clinical assessment. A key caveat is the upper GI mimic: a brisk upper GI bleed with rapid intestinal transit and haemodynamic instability can present as fresh PR bleeding. A raised urea (from digested blood) and shock out of proportion to the apparent lower source should prompt consideration of an OGD to exclude an upper GI cause. For confirmed LGIB, CT angiography is used for active/ongoing bleeding and colonoscopy for stable patients.
🚩 Haemodynamically unstable patients or those with ongoing bleeding need admission and resuscitation regardless of score. A massive-looking bleed with shock may be an upper GI source (look for raised urea) — consider upper endoscopy.
🎓 Oakland ≤ 8 identifies low-risk patients safe for outpatient care (validated, NICE-endorsed pathway). Haemoglobin carries the greatest weighting. Use CT angiography for active bleeding and colonoscopy for stable patients.

The Truelove & Witts criteria classify the severity of an acute ulcerative colitis (UC) flare as mild, moderate or severe. Their key role is to identify acute severe ulcerative colitis (ASUC) — a medical emergency needing hospital admission, IV steroids and a structured day-3 review to time rescue therapy or surgery. The memorable core is the “6 + 1” rule: ≥6 bloody stools per day PLUS any one systemic marker = severe.

1When to use it & what it defines
Apply at the bedside to any patient presenting with an acute UC flare (known or new diagnosis) to stratify severity and trigger the correct pathway. Severity rests on two things: stool frequency with blood, and the presence of systemic upset. Identifying severe disease is the whole point — it mandates emergency admission, because ASUC carries a real risk of toxic megacolon, perforation and colectomy.
2The systemic criteria (the “+1” features)
Alongside stool frequency, severe disease requires at least one of these four systemic markers. In practice: temperature, pulse, haemoglobin, ESR/CRP.
💩STOOL FREQUENCY
≥6 bloody stools per day is the threshold for severe
🌡️TEMPERATURE
Fever >37.8°C
💓PULSE
Tachycardia >90 bpm
🩸HAEMOGLOBIN
Anaemia: Hb <105 g/L
🔬ESR / CRP
ESR >30 mm/hr (or CRP raised)
3Classifying severity
MILD→<4 stools/day, little or no blood, NO systemic upset, normal ESR — often managed as outpatient
MODERATE→4–6 stools/day with minimal systemic features — between mild and severe
SEVERE (ASUC)→≥6 bloody stools/day PLUS ≥1 systemic feature — ADMIT, medical emergency
Systemic features = temp >37.8°C, pulse >90, Hb <105 g/L, ESR >30 (or raised CRP).
Only ONE systemic marker is needed alongside the ≥6 bloody stools to call it severe.
4Managing acute severe UC (ASUC)
A medical emergency — managed jointly by gastroenterology and colorectal surgery.
Admit for inpatient care with daily gastro and surgical input.
IV corticosteroids — IV hydrocortisone (e.g. 100 mg QDS) is first-line.
VTE prophylaxis — ASUC is highly prothrombotic; give LMWH despite rectal bleeding.
Stool chart to track frequency and blood; strict fluid/electrolyte balance.
Flexible sigmoidoscopy with biopsy (limited, unprepped — not full colonoscopy, which risks perforation) to confirm the diagnosis/severity and look for CMV.
Exclude infection — stool cultures and C. difficile toxin; consider CMV (flexible sigmoidoscopy/biopsy) in steroid-refractory cases.
Abdominal X-ray (AXR) to exclude toxic megacolon and perforation.
Daily bloods (FBC, CRP, U&E, albumin) and observations.
5Day-3 review — the Travis criteria
Response to IV steroids is formally assessed on day 3. Non-response predicts the need for colectomy and triggers escalation to rescue therapy or surgery.
Day 3: >8 stools/day→~85% will need colectomy — escalate now
Day 3: CRP >45 + 3–8 stools/day→~85% will need colectomy — escalate now
Steroid non-response→Rescue therapy: IV ciclosporin OR infliximab; if that fails or patient deteriorates → colectomy
🚩 Toxic megacolon (colonic dilatation >6 cm on AXR + systemic toxicity) is life-threatening with a high perforation risk — get early surgical review. Avoid antimotility, opioid and antispasmodic agents, which can precipitate or worsen it. A rigid, silent, distended abdomen or rising toxicity mandates urgent colectomy.
🎓 Remember the “6 + 1” rule: ≥6 bloody stools/day plus any single systemic marker (fever >37.8°C, pulse >90, Hb <105 g/L, ESR >30) = severe. The day-3 Travis review is the exam’s favourite decision point — it is where timely rescue therapy or surgery is decided.

The Hinchey classification stages acute complicated (perforated) diverticulitis by the extent of contamination seen on CT or at operation. It is a severity/anatomical grading — not a probability score — and its central job is to match the finding to the management, from antibiotics through percutaneous drainage to emergency resection. Escalating stage tracks escalating peritoneal soiling and mortality.

1When it is used & what it stages
Applied to acute complicated diverticulitis — i.e. diverticulitis with an abscess or perforation — to grade the degree of contamination. Uncomplicated diverticulitis (inflammation only, no abscess/perforation) sits outside the classification and is managed conservatively. The staging investigation is CT abdomen/pelvis (contrast), or direct operative findings. The stage then dictates whether the patient needs antibiotics, drainage, or theatre.
2The four stages (I–IV)
🫧STAGE I
Pericolic abscess/phlegmon confined to mesentery/colonic wall (Ia phlegmon; Ib pericolic abscess)
🩸STAGE II
Pelvic, distant intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal abscess (walled-off, remote from colon)
💧STAGE III
Generalised PURULENT peritonitis (ruptured abscess, NO communication with bowel lumen)
💩STAGE IV
Generalised FAECULENT peritonitis (free perforation with faecal contamination of the peritoneum)
I–II = contained collections (abscess/phlegmon).
III–IV = free generalised peritonitis — the difference between them is pus (III) vs faeces (IV).
3Stage → management
Uncomplicated (no stage)→Conservative — antibiotics per local/NICE guideline, often outpatient; some low-risk cases managed without antibiotics
Hinchey I / II, abscess ≤ 3–4 cm→IV antibiotics alone; monitor for response
Hinchey I / II, abscess > 3–4 cm→Antibiotics + radiological (percutaneous CT-guided) drainage
Hinchey III / IV→Emergency surgery — classically Hartmann's procedure (sigmoid colectomy + end colostomy) + sepsis resuscitation; laparoscopic lavage debated
4Interpretation & limitations
The stage is a snapshot that guides the threshold for intervention: contained disease (I–II) is increasingly treated non-operatively (antibiotics ± drainage), whereas free peritonitis (III–IV) mandates the operating theatre. Hartmann's remains the classic emergency operation for III/IV; primary resection with anastomosis (± defunctioning stoma) and laparoscopic lavage for purulent (III) disease are used in selected patients but remain debated. Limitations: the original classification predates modern CT (hence the Ia/Ib and other modifications), it captures anatomy not physiology, and it must always be read alongside the patient's haemodynamic and septic status.
🚩 Hinchey III/IV = generalised peritonitis + sepsis = a surgical emergency from free perforation. Faeculent peritonitis (IV) carries a high mortality. Do not delay: resuscitate for sepsis and arrange urgent surgery.
🎓 Remember the key split: III = purulent, IV = faeculent. CT is the staging investigation, and free air / faecal contamination → theatre.

Staging of colorectal cancer describes how far the tumour has spread, and is the single strongest predictor of prognosis and treatment. Two systems dominate: the historical Dukes classification (still examined for its clarity and memorable survival figures) and the current gold-standard TNM system, which drives modern stage grouping and adjuvant chemotherapy decisions.

1What it is & when it is used
Colorectal cancer is staged after diagnosis to guide management and estimate survival. Diagnosis is confirmed by colonoscopy + biopsy. Staging investigations include CT chest/abdomen/pelvis (distant spread, especially liver and lung), MRI rectum for local staging of rectal tumours (assessing circumferential resection margin and mesorectal nodes), and CEA (carcinoembryonic antigen) as a baseline tumour marker used to monitor recurrence. Dukes was devised in the 1930s for rectal cancer; TNM (tumour, node, metastasis) is now the international standard.
2Dukes classification & survival
Dukes stages the depth of invasion and nodal spread, and each stage carries a characteristic 5-year survival. The core mnemonic: A in the wall, B through the wall, C in the nodes, D distant.
🟢DUKES A
Confined to bowel wall — into but not through muscularis propria. No nodes. ~90%+ 5yr survival.
🔵DUKES B
Through the bowel wall (breaches muscularis propria/serosa) but no lymph nodes. ~65–70% 5yr survival.
🟠DUKES C
Regional lymph node involvement (C1 = nodes near primary; C2 = apical node). ~30–40% 5yr survival.
🔴DUKES D
Distant metastasis (later addition), e.g. liver. ~5–10% 5yr survival.
3TNM — the current standard
TNM describes tumour depth (T), regional nodes (N) and distant metastasis (M) independently.
T (tumour): Tis = carcinoma in situ; T1 = invades submucosa; T2 = invades muscularis propria; T3 = through muscularis into subserosa/pericolic tissue; T4 = through serosa (T4a) or into adjacent organs (T4b).
N (nodes): N0 = no regional nodes; N1 = 1–3 regional nodes; N2 = ≥4 regional nodes.
M (metastasis): M0 = none; M1 = distant metastasis present.
4Stage grouping, Dukes mapping & management
TNM categories combine into numbered stages, which map roughly onto Dukes and drive treatment.
Stage I (T1–2 N0 M0)→≈ Dukes A · ~90%+ survival · surgical resection alone
Stage II (T3–4 N0 M0)→≈ Dukes B · ~65–70% · surgery; adjuvant chemo considered if high-risk features
Stage III (any T, N1–2 M0)→≈ Dukes C · ~30–40% · surgery + adjuvant chemo (FOLFOX)
Stage IV (any T, any N, M1)→≈ Dukes D · ~5–10% · palliative or metastasis-directed chemo ± surgery (e.g. liver resection)
Surgery is the mainstay for localised disease; adjuvant FOLFOX chemotherapy is standard for stage III (node-positive) disease. Rectal cancers often receive neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy guided by MRI.
🚩 Earlier-stage detection saves lives: the NHS bowel cancer screening programme (FIT test) and the 2-week-wait referral criteria (e.g. iron-deficiency anaemia, change in bowel habit, rectal bleeding, abdominal mass) exist to catch tumours at Dukes A/B rather than C/D. The liver is the commonest site of distant metastasis — always scrutinise it on staging CT.
🎓 Dukes A→D maps to progressively worsening survival (≈90% → 5–10%). TNM is now the standard, but Dukes remains the memorable exam shorthand: "A in the wall, B through the wall, C in the nodes, D distant." Remember N1 = 1–3 nodes, N2 = ≥4 nodes, and that any node-positive disease is at least Stage III.

The Alvarado score (mnemonic MANTRELS) is a clinical scoring tool that estimates the likelihood of acute appendicitis in a patient presenting with right iliac fossa (RIF) pain. It combines symptoms, signs and two simple laboratory values into a score out of 10, helping to stratify patients into those who can be safely observed or discharged, those who warrant imaging, and those who should proceed to surgical referral. It is an adjunct to structured clinical assessment — not a substitute for it.

1When to use it & what it estimates
Apply it to the patient with undifferentiated RIF / lower abdominal pain where appendicitis is on the differential. It quantifies the pre-test probability of acute appendicitis and guides the next step: reassurance/observation, cross-sectional imaging, or surgical referral. It is quick, bedside, and needs only a history, an examination, a temperature and a full blood count.
2The components — MANTRELS (total 10)
🏃M — Migration
Migration of pain to the RIF (1 point)
🍽️A — Anorexia
Loss of appetite (1 point)
🤢N — Nausea
Nausea and/or vomiting (1 point)
✋T — Tenderness (RIF)
Tenderness in the RIF (2 points)
↩️R — Rebound
Rebound tenderness (1 point)
🌡️E — Elevated temp
Temperature ≥37.3°C (1 point)
🩸L — Leukocytosis
WCC >10 ×10&sup9;/L (2 points)
⬅️S — Shift to left
Neutrophilia / left shift (1 point)
Two components carry 2 points each — RIF Tenderness and Leukocytosis — making them the most heavily weighted.
The remaining six items score 1 point each; the maximum total is 10.
3Scoring bands & action
1–4→Appendicitis unlikely — consider discharge or an alternative diagnosis
5–6→Compatible with appendicitis — observe and/or consider imaging (USS/CT)
7–8→Probable appendicitis — surgical review
9–10→Highly likely — surgical referral
4Interpretation, limitations & clinical use
Best used to triage the next step: a low score supports observation, an intermediate score supports imaging, and a high score supports surgical referral — reducing negative appendicectomy rates and unnecessary scans.
Has lower specificity in women, where gynaecological mimics (ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion/cyst, pelvic inflammatory disease) inflate the score, and its performance is also weaker in children.
Should be combined with serial examination and, where uncertainty persists, imaging or diagnostic laparoscopy.
🚩 The score supports but does not replace clinical judgement or serial examination. A low score does not exclude appendicitis — particularly early, atypical or retrocaecal presentations. In women, exclude ectopic pregnancy (do a pregnancy test) and ovarian pathology; arrange CT/USS and consider diagnostic laparoscopy where the diagnosis remains uncertain.
🎓 Remember the mnemonic MANTRELS. The two double-weighted items are RIF Tenderness and Leukocytosis (2 points each) — the highest-yield components. Ultimately, appendicitis remains a clinical diagnosis; the Alvarado score only structures your reasoning.
RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__Hepatology:
Acute pancreatitis is graded for severity, not just diagnosed. The Glasgow-Imrie score (modified Glasgow) is a UK-favoured tool that uses eight laboratory and physiological variables assessed within 48 hours of admission to predict severe disease. A score of ≥3 predicts severe pancreatitis and should prompt escalation to HDU/ITU. Crucially, the degree of amylase or lipase rise diagnoses pancreatitis but tells you nothing about severity — severity is assessed with scores like this.

1WHEN & WHAT IT PREDICTS

Pancreatitis is diagnosed by clinical features plus amylase/lipase (typically >3× upper limit) or imaging. Once diagnosed, severity must be stratified to guide monitoring and level of care. The Glasgow-Imrie score is calculated using the worst values obtained within the first 48 hours. Common aetiology is captured by GET SMASHED (Gallstones, Ethanol, Trauma, Steroids, Mumps, Autoimmune, Scorpion sting, Hypercalcaemia/Hypertriglyceridaemia, ERCP, Drugs) — gallstones and ethanol are by far the most common.

Diagnose: amylase/lipase & clinical picture
Stratify severity: Glasgow-Imrie (≥3), APACHE II (≥8), CRP >150 at 48h
Image necrosis: contrast CT — CT Severity Index (Balthazar)
2THE COMPONENTS — mnemonic PANCREAS

Eight criteria, each scoring 1 point if met, assessed within 48h:

🫁P — PaO₂
< 8 kPa (hypoxia)
🎂A — Age
> 55 years
🩸N — Neutrophils
WCC > 15 × 10⁹/L
🦴C — Calcium
< 2 mmol/L
🫘R — Renal (urea)
Urea > 16 mmol/L
🧪E — Enzymes
LDH > 600 or AST > 200 IU/L
💧A — Albumin
< 32 g/L
🍬S — Sugar
Glucose > 10 mmol/L
3SCORING & THRESHOLDS

Add one point per criterion met (maximum 8).

Score 0–2→Predicted mild pancreatitis — ward-level supportive care & monitoring
Score ≥ 3→Predicts SEVERE pancreatitis — senior review, consider HDU/ITU

Other severity tools you should recognise:

APACHE II ≥ 8→Severe — generic ICU physiology score, usable at any time point
CRP > 150 at 48h→Marker of severe disease / pancreatic necrosis
Ranson score (US)→Alternative — measured at admission and again at 48h
4INTERPRETATION, IMAGING & MANAGEMENT

Severity scores guide level of care, not diagnosis. Contrast-enhanced CT is used to assess complications such as necrosis — graded by the CT Severity Index (Balthazar), which combines the degree of inflammation with the extent of necrosis. Core management is supportive:

Early aggressive IV fluid resuscitation (mainstay)
Analgesia & antiemetics
Close monitoring — urine output, observations, repeat bloods/ABG
