Treat the cause — e.g. ERCP for obstructing gallstones, alcohol withdrawal support
🚩 Severe acute pancreatitis (Glasgow-Imrie ≥3 / APACHE II ≥8) can progress to organ failure, pancreatic necrosis and multi-organ dysfunction. Escalate early for senior/ITU input, deliver early aggressive fluid resuscitation, and actively watch for complications — necrosis, pseudocyst, ARDS and AKI.
🎓 Remember the components with PANCREAS (PaO₂, Age, Neutrophils, Calcium, Renal/urea, Enzymes, Albumin, Sugar). High-yield trap: the degree of amylase rise does NOT correlate with severity — a modest amylase can accompany severe disease. Diagnose with enzymes; grade severity with a scoring system.

The Child-Pugh score and the MELD score both grade the severity of chronic liver disease and predict prognosis in cirrhosis, but they answer slightly different questions. Child-Pugh is the classic bedside grade of hepatic reserve, stratifying patients into Classes A, B and C to estimate survival and peri-operative/surgical risk. MELD (Model for End-stage Liver Disease) is a calculated logarithmic score derived purely from lab values that predicts 3-month mortality and is used to prioritise organ allocation for liver transplantation — the higher the MELD, the sicker the patient and the higher their place on the waiting list.

1WHEN TO USE THEM

Both are applied to patients with established cirrhosis / chronic liver disease to quantify severity rather than to diagnose it.

Child-Pugh — bedside grade of hepatic reserve; estimates 1- and 2-year survival and, classically, the risk of surgery/anaesthesia in a cirrhotic patient.
MELD — predicts short-term (3-month) mortality; used to rank patients for liver transplant listing and to prognosticate in decompensated disease and procedures such as TIPS.
2CHILD-PUGH COMPONENTS — "ABCDE"

Five variables, each scored 1–3 points. Remember them with ABCDE: Albumin, Bilirubin, Clotting (INR/prothrombin time), Distension (ascites), Encephalopathy.

🟡BILIRUBIN
<34 µmol/L = 1 · 34–50 = 2 · >50 = 3
🩸ALBUMIN
>35 g/L = 1 · 28–35 = 2 · <28 = 3
⏱️INR (CLOTTING)
<1.7 = 1 · 1.7–2.3 = 2 · >2.3 = 3 (prothrombin time)
💧ASCITES
None = 1 · Mild (diuretic-responsive) = 2 · Moderate–severe = 3
🧠ENCEPHALOPATHY
None = 1 · Grade 1–2 = 2 · Grade 3–4 = 3
3CHILD-PUGH SCORING & CLASSES

Add the five components for a total of 5–15, then convert to a class:

Class A: 5–6→Well-compensated disease · ~100% 1-yr / ~85% 2-yr survival · good surgical candidate
Class B: 7–9→Significant functional compromise · ~80% 1-yr / ~60% 2-yr survival · intermediate surgical risk
Class C: 10–15→Decompensated disease · ~45% 1-yr / ~35% 2-yr survival · poor prognosis, high surgical mortality — consider transplant
4MELD — TRANSPLANT PRIORITISATION

MELD is a calculated logarithmic score (range 6–40) using three objective labs — bilirubin, INR and creatinine. MELD-Na adds serum sodium, as hyponatraemia further worsens prognosis. Unlike Child-Pugh it avoids subjective variables (ascites, encephalopathy).

Higher MELD→Higher predicted 3-month mortality → higher priority on the transplant waiting list
MELD ≥ 15→Transplant survival benefit generally outweighs risk — a common listing threshold
Child-Pugh → classic bedside grade of severity and surgical/peri-operative risk.
MELD / MELD-Na → objective, lab-only score for transplant listing and short-term prognosis.
🚩 Signs of decompensation — variceal bleeding, ascites, hepatic encephalopathy and jaundice — signal a poor prognosis and push a patient toward Child-Pugh C and higher MELD. A high or rising MELD should prompt transplant referral. Always screen for hepatocellular carcinoma (surveillance USS ± AFP) and actively seek reversible precipitants (GI bleed, infection/SBP, constipation, sedatives, electrolyte disturbance) — the score never replaces clinical judgement.
🎓 Child-Pugh mnemonic "ABCDE": Albumin, Bilirubin, Clotting (INR), Distension (ascites), Encephalopathy — two clinical, three lab. MELD = Bilirubin, INR, Creatinine (± Na) — all objective labs, used for transplant allocation. A neat way to keep them apart: Child-Pugh has the two subjective variables (ascites, encephalopathy); MELD is lab-only.

The King's College Criteria identify patients with acute liver failure (ALF) whose prognosis is so poor that they should be referred for urgent liver transplantation. Acute liver failure is defined as hepatic encephalopathy plus coagulopathy (INR > 1.5) developing in a patient without pre-existing liver disease. Because outcomes without transplant are dismal once these thresholds are crossed, the criteria are used to decide who needs a transplant centre — split into a paracetamol-induced pathway and a non-paracetamol pathway.

1WHAT IS ACUTE LIVER FAILURE & WHEN TO USE THE CRITERIA
ALF = rapid loss of hepatic function with encephalopathy + coagulopathy (INR > 1.5) in someone with a previously normal liver. Paracetamol overdose is the commonest UK cause. The King's Criteria are applied once ALF is established to flag patients unlikely to survive with medical therapy alone, prompting early discussion with a liver transplant unit. There are two separate rule sets depending on aetiology.
Encephalopathy grades: I (altered mood/attention) → II (drowsy, confused, asterixis) → III (marked confusion, rousable) → IV (coma).
Coagulopathy reflects failure of hepatic synthetic function — do not correct the INR routinely, as it is a key prognostic marker.
2THE VARIABLES — PARACETAMOL vs NON-PARACETAMOL
Each pathway uses a different set of markers. The paracetamol pathway hinges on acidosis or a triad of PT, creatinine and encephalopathy; the non-paracetamol pathway uses PT alone or a combination of age, aetiology, jaundice duration, PT and bilirubin.
🧪PARACETAMOL: pH
Arterial pH < 7.3 after adequate fluid resuscitation (> 24 h post-ingestion)
🩸PARACETAMOL: PT
PT > 100 s (INR > 6.5)
🫘PARACETAMOL: CREATININE
Creatinine > 300 µmol/L
🧠PARACETAMOL: ENCEPHALOPATHY
Grade III / IV hepatic encephalopathy (± lactate > 3.5 early / > 3.0 post-resuscitation in some versions)
🎂NON-PCM: AGE
Age < 10 or > 40 years
🧬NON-PCM: AETIOLOGY
Seronegative hepatitis, drug reaction, or halothane
🟡NON-PCM: JAUNDICE DURATION
Jaundice > 7 days before onset of encephalopathy
🩸NON-PCM: PT
PT > 50 s (INR > 3.5)
🟤NON-PCM: BILIRUBIN
Bilirubin > 300 µmol/L
3THRESHOLDS — WHO GETS LISTED FOR TRANSPLANT
Meeting the relevant rule set predicts poor prognosis and triggers transplant referral.
PARACETAMOL: arterial pH < 7.3→List for transplant (after adequate fluid resuscitation, > 24 h post-ingestion)
PARACETAMOL: PT > 100 s AND creatinine > 300 AND grade III/IV encephalopathy→The triad — all three together → list for transplant
NON-PARACETAMOL: PT > 100 s (INR > 6.5) alone→List for transplant regardless of other variables
NON-PARACETAMOL: any 3 of 5 (age, aetiology, jaundice > 7 d, PT > 50 s, bilirubin > 300)→List for transplant
4MANAGEMENT & CLINICAL USE
ALF is managed on ITU alongside prognostication. Core measures: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) — give in paracetamol overdose and consider even in non-paracetamol ALF; supportive intensive care; active treatment of cerebral oedema / raised ICP; correction of hypoglycaemia; and vigilance for infection and bleeding. The criteria are highly specific but only moderately sensitive — failing to meet them does not guarantee survival, so they guide but never replace clinical judgement and specialist input.
Contact the transplant unit early — deterioration can be rapid and a window for transfer may close.
Serial arterial pH, lactate, INR, creatinine and encephalopathy grade are tracked to detect a patient crossing threshold.
🚩 Acute liver failure is an ITU emergency — watch for cerebral oedema and raised ICP, hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy and infection. Refer to a transplant centre EARLY and do not wait for every criterion to be met. Give NAC even in non-paracetamol ALF. The criteria are specific but not perfectly sensitive — a patient can still die despite not meeting them.
🎓 Paracetamol pathway = pH < 7.3 OR the triad (PT > 100 s + creatinine > 300 + grade III/IV encephalopathy). The King's College Criteria identify who needs a transplant — they are a prognostic/referral tool, not a diagnostic one.

Two complementary scores steer corticosteroid decisions in severe alcoholic hepatitis. Maddrey's Discriminant Function (DF) is calculated at presentation to decide who to treat — a DF ≥32 defines severe disease with high 28-day/90-day mortality. The Lille score is then calculated at day 7 of steroid therapy to decide whether the treatment is working — a Lille >0.45 identifies non-responders in whom steroids should be stopped.

1MADDREY DF — WHO TO TREAT

Calculated at presentation to grade severity and select patients for corticosteroids. Formula: DF = 4.6 × (patient PT − control PT) + serum bilirubin (mg/dL). A DF ≥32 indicates severe alcoholic hepatitis carrying high short-term mortality (roughly 30–50% at 28–90 days untreated), and is the classic threshold to consider prednisolone 40 mg daily — provided there is no contraindication.

Uses prothrombin time prolongation (patient minus laboratory control PT), not INR.
Bilirubin must be in mg/dL — divide a µmol/L value by ~17.1 to convert.
2DF COMPONENTS
🩸PT PROLONGATION
patient PT − control PT (seconds), weighted ×4.6
🟡BILIRUBIN
serum bilirubin in mg/dL, added directly
3DF THRESHOLD & ACTION
DF < 32→Non-severe — supportive care, steroids not indicated
DF ≥ 32→SEVERE — consider prednisolone 40 mg/day if no contraindication (active infection, GI bleed, renal failure)
🚩 Before starting steroids you MUST exclude and treat active infection/sepsis and GI bleeding — corticosteroids worsen sepsis and can be fatal. Screen and treat first, then reassess.
4LILLE SCORE — IS TREATMENT WORKING (DAY 7)

Calculated after 7 days of corticosteroids to assess response. It combines baseline severity with the fall in bilirubin from day 0 to day 7 — the key dynamic variable. A poor bilirubin response predicts steroid futility.

🎂AGE
older age worsens prognosis
🧪ALBUMIN
day 0 — synthetic liver function
🟡BILIRUBIN (DAY 0)
baseline bilirubin
📉Δ BILIRUBIN
change day 0 → day 7 (the decisive variable)
🫘CREATININE
renal function (hepatorenal risk)
🩸PROTHROMBIN TIME
coagulopathy / synthetic function
5LILLE THRESHOLD & ACTION
Lille ≤ 0.45→RESPONDER — continue steroids to complete 28-day course
Lille > 0.45→NON-RESPONDER (~75% 6-month mortality) — STOP steroids (futile, ongoing infection risk); consider palliation / transplant assessment
DF selects who to treat; Lille tells you if it is working.
Stopping steroids in non-responders avoids weeks of needless immunosuppression and sepsis risk.
6ALTERNATIVES & MANAGEMENT CONTEXT
GAHS (Glasgow Alcoholic Hepatitis Score) — age, WCC, urea, PT ratio, bilirubin; alternative severity tool guiding steroid benefit.
MELD — bilirubin, INR, creatinine; also prognosticates and is used for transplant listing.

Alongside scoring, management includes nutritional support (high-calorie/protein), thiamine for Wernicke's prophylaxis, active screening for and treatment of infection/sepsis before steroids, correction of AKI/electrolytes, and alcohol abstinence with withdrawal management. N-acetylcysteine may be used as an adjunct to steroids in some regimens.

🎓 High-yield: DF ≥32 = severe → treat (prednisolone 40 mg). Lille >0.45 at day 7 = non-responder → STOP steroids.

The West Haven criteria are the standard clinical grading system for the severity of hepatic encephalopathy (HE) — the reversible neuropsychiatric syndrome of liver failure. HE arises when the failing liver (or portosystemic shunting) can no longer clear ammonia and other gut-derived neurotoxins, which cross the blood–brain barrier and cause cerebral dysfunction ranging from subtle cognitive change to deep coma. West Haven stratifies this spectrum into five grades (0–4), guiding urgency, disposition and the search for a precipitant.

1When to use it & the pathophysiology
Use West Haven to grade severity in any patient with known chronic liver disease or acute liver failure who develops altered cognition, behaviour or consciousness. The mechanism is failure of hepatic detoxification: ammonia (NH₃) produced by gut bacteria bypasses or overwhelms the liver, accumulates, and — along with other neurotoxins and neuroinflammation — drives astrocyte swelling and cerebral dysfunction. Grading is a bedside clinical tool; grade 0 (covert) requires psychometric testing to detect.
2Covert vs overt HE
The first clinically useful split is between covert (grades 0–1, easily missed) and overt (grades 2–4, clinically obvious) disease.
🔬GRADE 0 (covert)
Minimal HE — no clinical signs; detectable only on psychometric testing
😴GRADES 1–2 (mild–moderate)
Altered sleep, short attention, asterixis, then lethargy, disorientation to time & personality change
🛌GRADES 3–4 (severe–coma)
Somnolence/stupor (grade 3) to unresponsive coma (grade 4) — airway at risk
3Grade → clinical features
Grade 0→Minimal/covert — normal exam; only psychometric abnormality
Grade 1→Trivial lack of awareness, shortened attention, altered sleep, mild asterixis, impaired addition/subtraction
Grade 2→Lethargy/apathy, disorientation to time, obvious personality change, inappropriate behaviour, asterixis, dyspraxia
Grade 3→Somnolence to semi-stupor but responsive to stimuli, gross disorientation, confusion, bizarre behaviour
Grade 4→Coma — unresponsive to pain and stimuli
4Precipitants & management
HE is usually triggered — always hunt the precipitant.
Infection (esp. spontaneous bacterial peritonitis — do an ascitic tap)
GI bleeding (large protein load to the gut)
Constipation and dehydration/diuretics
Electrolyte disturbance — hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia
Sedatives/opioids and excess dietary protein load
Renal failure; recent TIPSS shunt
Management: identify and treat the precipitant first; lactulose titrated to 2–3 soft stools/day (reduces ammonia production and absorption); rifaximin (non-absorbable antibiotic, reduces ammonia-producing gut bacteria) for prevention of recurrence; supportive care and treat any infection.
🚩 Always search for a precipitant — especially infection/SBP (do an ascitic tap) and GI bleeding. Grade 3–4 = airway risk and may need ITU/intubation. Asterixis (liver flap) is the classic bedside sign of overt HE.
🎓 Grades 0–1 = covert HE, grades 2–4 = overt. First-line treatment is lactulose + treat the precipitant; add rifaximin for secondary prevention of recurrent episodes.

When a drug injures the liver (drug-induced liver injury, DILI), two tools are used together: Hy's Law flags cases at high risk of serious/fatal outcome, and RUCAM (Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method) scores how likely a specific drug is the culprit. Hy's Law is a key safety signal in drug trials: hepatocellular injury with jaundice and no other cause carries roughly 10% or higher mortality from acute liver failure.

1CLASSIFY THE PATTERN OF INJURY (R RATIO)

Before applying Hy's Law, define the injury pattern using the R ratio = (ALT ÷ ULN) ÷ (ALP ÷ ULN). This separates a hepatocyte-killing (dangerous) picture from a bile-duct (cholestatic) picture.

🔥Hepatocellular
ALT-predominant, R ≥ 5 — the pattern Hy's Law applies to
🟰Mixed
2 < R < 5 — features of both
🟡Cholestatic
ALP-predominant, R ≤ 2 — bile flow problem, not Hy's Law
Hy's Law requires a hepatocellular (ALT-driven) picture — a big ALP rise points to cholestasis/obstruction instead.
ULN = upper limit of normal for that lab.
2HY'S LAW — THE THREE COMPONENTS

All three must be present. Together they mean hepatocytes are dying and the liver can no longer clear bilirubin — a failing organ, not a nuisance transaminitis.

🩸ALT / AST ≥ 3× ULN
Hepatocellular injury (transaminitis)
🟠Bilirubin ≥ 2× ULN
Jaundice — impaired hepatic function
🚫No other cause
No obstruction, viral, autoimmune, or significant ALP rise
ALT ≥ 3× + bili ≥ 2× + hepatocellular + no other cause→Hy's Law positive: ~10%+ mortality — STOP the drug, escalate
ALT ≥ 3× but bilirubin normal→Not Hy's Law — monitor, but far lower risk
Marked ALP rise (cholestatic, R ≤ 2)→Hy's Law does not apply — investigate obstruction
3RUCAM — CAUSALITY SCORING

Hy's Law says how dangerous; RUCAM says was it this drug? It is a structured points system that yields a probability category. Domains scored:

Time to onset — a plausible latency between starting the drug and injury.
Course after stopping (dechallenge) — do the LFTs fall once the drug is withdrawn?
Risk factors — age, alcohol.
Concomitant drugs — other hepatotoxic agents on board.
Exclusion of other causes — viral hepatitis, autoimmune, biliary, ischaemia.
Previous hepatotoxicity — is the drug a known liver offender?
Rechallenge — recurrence on re-exposure (strongest evidence, rarely done deliberately).
RUCAM ≥ 9→Highly probable
6–8→Probable
3–5→Possible
1–2→Unlikely
≤ 0→Excluded
4CULPRITS & MANAGEMENT
Co-amoxiclav — the commonest cause of DILI (often cholestatic, delayed onset).
Flucloxacillin — classic cholestatic DILI.
Anti-TB drugs — isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide.
Statins, methotrexate — monitored transaminitis.
Paracetamol — dose-dependent hepatocellular necrosis.
Herbal / complementary — often unrecognised.
Suspected DILI→STOP the culprit drug — the single most important step
After stopping→Supportive care; monitor LFTs to resolution
Paracetamol overdose→N-acetylcysteine (NAC)
🚩 A positive Hy's Law (ALT/AST ≥ 3× ULN + total bilirubin ≥ 2× ULN, hepatocellular pattern, no other cause) predicts serious or fatal DILI — stop the drug and escalate. You MUST exclude other causes first: biliary obstruction (imaging), viral hepatitis, autoimmune liver disease and ischaemia. A significant ALP rise means a cholestatic picture — Hy's Law does not apply.
🎓 Hy's Law = transaminitis + jaundice from hepatocellular DILI = danger. Co-amoxiclav is the commonest cause of DILI. Remember the split of duties: Hy's Law grades severity/prognosis, RUCAM grades causality (was it the drug?).

Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) usually arises in a cirrhotic liver, so its management must weigh tumour burden, liver function and the patient together, not the cancer alone. Two frameworks dominate finals: the BCLC (Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer) system, which links stage directly to treatment and prognosis, and the Milan criteria, which decide who is eligible for liver transplant.

1Context — where HCC comes from & how it is caught

HCC almost always complicates cirrhosis — hepatitis B, hepatitis C, alcohol-related liver disease and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) are the major drivers. Because early tumours are silent, at-risk cirrhotics enter surveillance.

Surveillance: 6-monthly liver ultrasound (USS), ± serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), in patients with cirrhosis.
Diagnosis is often radiological: a nodule showing characteristic arterial-phase enhancement with venous/delayed washout on multiphase CT or MRI (LI-RADS) is diagnostic — biopsy is frequently avoided.
Why it matters: only around a third of patients present at a curative stage, so catching disease early through surveillance is the single biggest lever on outcome.
2BCLC — the inputs it integrates

BCLC is a staging and treatment algorithm. It combines three domains to place a patient in one of five stages (0, A, B, C, D):

🎯Tumour burden
Number & size of nodules; vascular invasion; extrahepatic spread
🩸Liver function
Child-Pugh class (A preserved → C decompensated)
🚶Performance status
ECOG PS 0 (fully active) → PS 3-4 (bedbound)
3BCLC stages → treatment
0️⃣Stage 0 — Very early
Single nodule <2 cm, preserved function, PS 0 → ablation or resection
🅰️Stage A — Early
Single tumour, or ≤3 nodules each ≤3 cm, PS 0 → resection, transplant or ablation (curative)
🅱️Stage B — Intermediate
Multinodular, PS 0, preserved function → transarterial chemoembolisation (TACE)
🆑Stage C — Advanced
Portal (vascular) invasion, extrahepatic spread, or PS 1-2 → systemic therapy
🅳Stage D — Terminal
Child-Pugh C or PS 3-4 → best supportive / palliative care

The stage-to-action mapping, distilled:

BCLC 0 / A→Curative intent — ablation, resection or transplant
BCLC B→TACE (transarterial chemoembolisation)
BCLC C→Systemic therapy — atezolizumab + bevacizumab (1st line), or sorafenib / lenvatinib
BCLC D→Best supportive care (median survival <3 months)
4Milan criteria — transplant eligibility

The Milan criteria identify HCC patients who will do well after liver transplant (which treats both the tumour and the underlying cirrhosis). A patient is within Milan if their imaging fits one of the two tumour patterns and there is no spread:

Single tumour ≤5 cm→Within Milan (if no invasion/spread)
Up to 3 tumours, each ≤3 cm→Within Milan (if no invasion/spread)
No extrahepatic spread AND no vascular invasion→Mandatory for eligibility — either pattern above must also meet this
Within Milan→Transplant eligible — good post-transplant survival & low recurrence
🚩 BCLC is powerful because it ties stage to treatment to prognosis in one algorithm — but that means liver function and performance status can override tumour size (a small tumour in Child-Pugh C is still Stage D). Only about a third of patients present at a curative stage, so 6-monthly surveillance in cirrhosis is the key to catching HCC early — do not wait for symptoms.
🎓 Milan = 1 lesion ≤5 cm OR ≤3 lesions each ≤3 cm, with no vascular invasion and no extrahepatic spread → transplant eligible. For BCLC, remember the ladder: 0/A curative, B TACE, C systemic, D supportive.
RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__Alcohol, Sepsis:
The CIWA-Ar (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol, revised) is a validated 10-item bedside scale that quantifies the severity of alcohol withdrawal. Its main purpose is to guide symptom-triggered benzodiazepine dosing — medicating according to the patient's actual withdrawal burden rather than a blind fixed schedule. Each item is scored (most 0–7, orientation 0–4) for a maximum of 67; higher scores mean more severe withdrawal and a higher risk of seizures and delirium tremens.

1When to use it & what it estimates
Used in patients known or suspected to be in alcohol withdrawal (dependent drinkers who stop or cut down). It does not diagnose withdrawal — it grades its severity so that treatment can be titrated. Scores are repeated (e.g. hourly) to track the withdrawal trajectory and response to benzodiazepines. Understanding the timeline helps anticipate risk: tremor/anxiety at 6–12h, withdrawal seizures at 12–48h, alcoholic hallucinosis at 12–24h, and delirium tremens (DTs) at 48–72h.
2The 10 components
🤢Nausea / vomiting
0–7
🤝Tremor
0–7, arms extended
💦Paroxysmal sweats
0–7
😰Anxiety
0–7
😣Agitation
0–7
🐛Tactile disturbances
0–7: paraesthesia, itching, bugs on skin
👂Auditory disturbances
0–7
👁️Visual disturbances
0–7
🤕Headache / fullness in head
0–7
🧭Orientation / clouding of sensorium
0–4 (the only 0–4 item)
3Scoring bands & management
< 8–10→Minimal / mild withdrawal — medication not usually needed
10–15→Mild–moderate withdrawal
16–20→Moderate withdrawal
> 20→Severe withdrawal — high risk of seizures / DTs; treat and escalate
Symptom-triggered regimen: give a benzodiazepine (e.g. chlordiazepoxide, diazepam or lorazepam) whenever CIWA ≥ 8–10, then reassess and re-score — the patient is only medicated as much as the withdrawal demands.
Fixed-dose reducing regimen: a pre-set tapering benzodiazepine schedule (e.g. reducing chlordiazepoxide over several days) given regardless of score — simpler and safer where monitoring is limited or in the community.
4Wider management & limitations
Benzodiazepines are the mainstay of treatment (cross-tolerant with alcohol; reduce seizure and DT risk).
Parenteral thiamine (IV Pabrinex) BEFORE any glucose, to prevent precipitating Wernicke's encephalopathy; plus fluids and close monitoring.
Limitation: CIWA relies on subjective, communicable symptoms — it is unreliable in patients who cannot report symptoms (intubated, delirious, non-English-speaking) and does not replace clinical judgement.
🚩 Delirium tremens is a medical emergency (confusion, autonomic instability and hallucinations at 48–72h; mortality up to ~15% if untreated). Always give parenteral thiamine before any glucose to avoid precipitating Wernicke's encephalopathy. Use lorazepam in preference in significant liver impairment (no active metabolites, safer with reduced hepatic clearance).
🎓 Two lines examiners love: a CIWA-Ar of ≥ 8–10 is the trigger for a symptom-triggered benzodiazepine dose — and thiamine always goes in before glucose.

Sepsis is a time-critical medical emergency. Under the Sepsis-3 definitions, sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection — operationalised as an acute rise in the SOFA score of ≥2 points attributable to infection. qSOFA is a rapid bedside screen to flag patients at higher risk of poor outcomes, and the Sepsis Six is the resuscitation bundle to be delivered within the first hour.

1Definitions — sepsis vs septic shock

Sepsis-3 reframed sepsis around organ dysfunction rather than the older SIRS criteria. Infection alone is not sepsis; it becomes sepsis when the host response causes measurable organ dysfunction.

Sepsis→Suspected/confirmed infection + acute rise in SOFA ≥2
Septic shock→Sepsis + vasopressors needed for MAP ≥65 mmHg AND lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation

Septic shock identifies a subset with profound circulatory, cellular and metabolic derangement and a substantially higher mortality.

2qSOFA — the bedside screen

qSOFA (quick SOFA) needs no bloods and can be scored at the bedside in seconds. One point each for three variables:

🫁Respiratory rate
≥22 breaths/min = 1 point
🧠Mentation
Altered mental state, GCS <15 = 1 point
🩸Systolic BP
≤100 mmHg = 1 point
qSOFA ≥2→Higher risk of poor outcome — escalate, assess for organ dysfunction, consider full SOFA and critical care review

qSOFA is a prompt to think and act, not a rule-out: a low score does not exclude sepsis in a patient who looks unwell.

3SOFA — the full organ-dysfunction score

The Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) grades dysfunction across six organ systems, each scored 0–4 (max 24). It requires investigations and is used mainly in critical care; an acute rise of ≥2 defines the organ dysfunction of sepsis.

🫁Respiration
PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio
🩸Coagulation
Platelet count
🫘Liver
Bilirubin
🫀Cardiovascular
MAP & vasopressor requirement
🧠CNS
Glasgow Coma Scale
💧Renal
Creatinine or urine output
Each system scores 0 (normal) to 4 (most deranged).
Baseline SOFA is assumed 0 unless known chronic organ dysfunction.
Rising SOFA tracks deterioration and correlates with mortality.
4Sepsis Six — the 1-hour bundle (BUFALO)

The Sepsis Six is a nurse/doctor-deliverable bundle to be completed within 1 hour of recognition. Remember it as 3 IN and 3 OUT (mnemonic BUFALO).

💨IN · Oxygen
High-flow O₂ to target saturations
💧IN · IV fluids
IV crystalloid bolus
💊IN · IV antibiotics
Broad-spectrum, after cultures
🧫OUT · Cultures
Blood cultures before antibiotics
🧪OUT · Lactate
Measure serum lactate
🚽OUT · Urine output
Monitor output, catheterise if needed
Lactate >2 mmol/L→Marker of hypoperfusion — reassess and repeat after fluids
Lactate >4 mmol/L or persisting hypotension→High risk — urgent senior/critical care input, consider vasopressors
🚩 Sepsis is a time-critical emergency — deliver the Sepsis Six within 1 hour (the ‘golden hour’). Lactate >2 mmol/L (especially >4) and hypotension signal shock and demand escalation. Source control (e.g. drainage of collections, removal of infected lines) is essential and antibiotics alone may not suffice. In the UK, NEWS2 is the standard track-and-trigger screen; a raised score should prompt sepsis screening. Scores support but never replace clinical judgement.
🎓 High-yield: Sepsis Six = 3 IN (Oxygen, IV Fluids, IV Antibiotics) + 3 OUT (blood Cultures, Lactate, Urine output) — mnemonic BUFALO. qSOFA ≥2 (of RR ≥22, altered mentation, SBP ≤100) flags a high-risk patient. Septic shock = vasopressors to keep MAP ≥65 + lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluids.

The National Early Warning Score 2 (NEWS2) is the UK national standard track-and-trigger physiological score, endorsed by the Royal College of Physicians and NHS England for detecting acute clinical deterioration in acutely ill adults. It aggregates seven bedside physiological parameters into a single number (each scored 0–3) that flags patients at risk of deterioration, cardiac arrest, unplanned ICU admission and death — and is the recommended screen to prompt sepsis consideration.

1When to use it & what it predicts

Use NEWS2 at every set of routine observations in any acutely unwell adult (≥16 years, not pregnant) on the ward, in ED and in the community/ambulance setting. It standardises the detection of deterioration and drives a graded escalation response. It is not validated in pregnancy, in children, or in patients on end-of-life pathways. As a screen it estimates the risk of near-term deterioration; a score of ≥5 should specifically prompt clinicians to think sepsis and screen for it alongside senior review.

2The seven parameters

Each parameter contributes 0–3 points; the physiological extremes score highest.

🌬️Respiratory rate
breaths/min; ≤8 or ≥25 score 3
🩸SpO₂ — Scale 1
standard target 96%; ≤91% scores 3
🫁SpO₂ — Scale 2
hypercapnic risk (COPD), target 88–92%
💨Supplemental O₂
air = 0, any oxygen = 2
🩺Systolic BP
mmHg; ≤90 or ≥220 score 3
❤️Pulse rate
bpm; ≤40 or ≥131 score 3
🧠Consciousness (ACVPU)
Alert = 0; new Confusion/V/P/U = 3
🌡️Temperature
°C; ≤35.0 scores 3

Two changes distinguish NEWS2 from the original NEWS1: the addition of SpO₂ Scale 2 for patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure (target saturation 88–92%), and the change of the consciousness scale from AVPU to ACVPU, where new-onset Confusion/delirium (C) now scores 3.

3Scoring bands & escalation

The seven parameter scores are summed to an aggregate (0–20). Both the total and any single high (red) parameter drive the response.

Total 0–4 (LOW)→Routine ward monitoring; minimum 12-hourly observations, registered nurse assesses
Any single parameter = 3 (RED)→LOW–MEDIUM; urgent review by clinician competent in acute illness, min 1-hourly obs
Total 5–6 (MEDIUM)→Urgent review by clinician; consider sepsis; escalate to team with critical-care skills; min hourly obs
Total ≥7 (HIGH)→Emergency assessment by critical-care team; continuous monitoring; usually transfer to higher level of care
4Sepsis screening & clinical use
NEWS2 ≥5 is the recommended trigger to actively screen for and consider sepsis in any patient with known or suspected infection, and to seek senior/clinician review.
The score enhances communication (a single objective number for handover and escalation) and detects deterioration earlier, but it does not diagnose a cause — it prompts assessment.
A rising trend over serial observations is as important as any single value; act on the trajectory, not just the isolated number.
🚩 NEWS2 ≥5, or any single parameter scoring 3 (red score), mandates escalation and active consideration of sepsis. Use SpO₂ Scale 2 (target 88–92%) only for patients with confirmed risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure (e.g. COPD) and only on a senior clinical decision — do not over-oxygenate. NEWS2 aids but never replaces clinical judgement: a worrying patient with a low score still warrants review.
🎓 NEWS2 ≥5 = think sepsis + escalate. The two hallmark features that separate NEWS2 from NEWS1 are the ACVPU scale scoring new Confusion (C) as 3, and the addition of SpO₂ Scale 2 for hypercapnic-risk patients.

The ATLS classification of haemorrhagic shock stratifies acute blood loss into four classes (I–IV) by the estimated volume lost and the body’s physiological response. For a typical 70 kg adult with a circulating blood volume of ~5 L, it links percentage blood loss to heart rate, blood pressure, pulse pressure, respiratory rate, urine output and mental state — giving a rapid bedside estimate of how much blood a trauma patient has lost and how urgently they need resuscitation.

1When to use it & what it estimates
Used in the circulation (C) assessment of a trauma primary survey to gauge the severity of haemorrhage from the pattern of vital signs. It estimates blood loss as a percentage of total blood volume (~5 L in a 70 kg adult) and predicts how close a patient is to decompensation. It guides urgency of haemorrhage control and blood product resuscitation — not a fixed diagnostic score but a physiological framework.
2The four classes
🩸CLASS I
<15% loss (<750 mL) · HR <100 · normal BP · normal pulse pressure · RR 14–20 · urine >30 mL/hr · normal/slightly anxious — fully compensated
🫀CLASS II
15–30% (750–1500 mL) · HR 100–120 · normal systolic BP but narrowed pulse pressure (raised diastolic) · RR 20–30 · urine 20–30 mL/hr · mildly anxious
⚠️CLASS III
30–40% (1500–2000 mL) · HR 120–140 · decreased systolic BP · narrowed pulse pressure · RR 30–40 · urine 5–15 mL/hr · anxious/confused
🆘CLASS IV
>40% (>2000 mL) · HR >140 · decreased BP · negligible pulse pressure · RR >35 · negligible urine · confused/lethargic — immediately life-threatening
3Reading the signs: class → physiology
Class I→Compensated — vitals essentially normal; equivalent to donating a unit of blood
Class II→Tachycardia + narrowed pulse pressure (rising diastolic from vasoconstriction) — the earliest reliable signs
Class III→Systolic BP now falls — overt decompensation; most patients need blood
Class IV→Peri-arrest — negligible urine and pulse pressure, obtunded; activate major haemorrhage protocol
Tachycardia and a narrowing pulse pressure precede hypotension — treat them as the alarm, not a normal BP.
Mental status and urine output track end-organ perfusion and deteriorate progressively across the classes.
4Management & limitations
Control the haemorrhage — direct pressure, tourniquet, splint pelvis/long bones, surgery or interventional radiology; treat the source.
IV access — two large-bore (14–16G) cannulae; send bloods including crossmatch.
Balanced resuscitation — activate the major haemorrhage protocol; give blood products in balanced ratios, use permissive hypotension in penetrating/uncontrolled trauma, and give tranexamic acid within 3 hours.
Fit young adult→Compensates well — may maintain systolic BP until class III, so a normal BP does not exclude major loss
🚩 Hypotension is a LATE sign. Young, fit patients vasoconstrict and maintain systolic BP until they have lost ~30–40% of their volume (class III) — do not be reassured by a normal BP. Class III/IV is immediately life-threatening: activate the major haemorrhage protocol. Beta-blockers (blunt tachycardia), pregnancy (increased volume masks loss until sudden decompensation) and athletes/elderly can all mask or distort the expected signs.
🎓 Remember the sequence: pulse pressure narrows early (class II, from a rising diastolic), systolic BP drops late (class III). Tachycardia + narrowing pulse pressure come before hypotension, while mental status and urine output track perfusion throughout.

The Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool (MUST) is a validated 5-step tool used to identify adults who are malnourished or at risk of malnutrition. It is applied on hospital admission and in the community, and combines three scored components — BMI, unplanned weight loss, and an acute disease effect — which are summed to give an overall risk category and a linked management pathway.

1WHEN TO USE IT
MUST screens all adults for malnutrition risk — routinely on hospital admission (and weekly thereafter), on admission to care homes, and in community/GP settings. It does not diagnose malnutrition; it flags who needs a nutritional care plan or dietitian referral. Malnutrition worsens clinical outcomes: impaired wound healing, reduced immunity, muscle wasting, longer admissions and higher mortality.
2THE THREE COMPONENTS
⚖️BMI (kg/m²)
>20 = 0 pts · 18.5–20 = 1 pt · <18.5 = 2 pts
📉WEIGHT LOSS
Unplanned loss over 3–6 months: <5% = 0 · 5–10% = 1 · >10% = 2 pts
🤒ACUTE DISEASE
Add 2 pts if acutely ill AND no / likely no nutritional intake for >5 days
If height/weight cannot be measured, use surrogate measures (ulna length, mid-upper arm circumference) and subjective criteria.
The acute-disease component is rare in the community and mostly applies to unwell inpatients.
3SCORING & RISK CATEGORY
Sum the three components for an overall score, then follow the linked pathway:
0→LOW risk — routine care; repeat screening (hospital weekly, care homes monthly, community annually in high-risk groups)
1→MEDIUM risk — observe; document dietary intake for 3 days; if adequate, repeat screening; if concern, follow local policy
≥2→HIGH risk — TREAT: refer to dietitian / nutrition support team, set goals, increase & support intake, monitor and review
4MANAGEMENT & NUTRITIONAL SUPPORT
High-risk patients need active nutritional support, escalating by the “if the gut works, use it” principle:
Oral — food fortification, encouragement, oral nutritional supplement drinks (ONS).
Enteral — nasogastric (NG) or gastrostomy (PEG) feeding when the gut is functional but oral intake is inadequate/unsafe.
Parenteral (TPN) — reserved for when the gut is unusable or inaccessible.
Set nutritional goals, monitor intake, weight and biochemistry, and review the plan regularly.
🚩 Refeeding syndrome — a life-threatening shift in fluids/electrolytes when feeding is reintroduced. High risk if little/no intake >5 days, low BMI, significant weight loss, alcohol excess, or low baseline phosphate/potassium/magnesium. Features: hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, thiamine deficiency and fluid overload. Prevent: start feeding cautiously (e.g. ~10 kcal/kg/day, building up slowly), give thiamine and B vitamins before and during feeding, and replace phosphate, potassium and magnesium with close electrolyte monitoring.
🎓 MUST = BMI + weight loss + acute disease effect. Score all patients on admission. A total of ≥2 = high risk → refer to dietitian and treat. Remember 0 = observe/repeat, 1 = document intake, ≥2 = act — and always ask “is this patient at risk of refeeding?” before starting feed.

Pressure ulcer (pressure injury) risk assessment tools flag inpatients at risk of skin breakdown from sustained pressure over bony prominences, so preventive measures can start before damage occurs. Two dominant scales are examined: the Waterlow score (UK-standard, where a HIGHER score means HIGHER risk) and the Braden scale (widely used internationally, which runs the OPPOSITE way – a LOWER score means HIGHER risk). Both are aids to structured judgement, not diagnoses; the aim is to trigger the SSKIN prevention bundle in those flagged.

1When to use & what it estimates
Assess pressure ulcer risk on admission and reassess regularly and after any change in condition, transfer, or surgery. The score estimates a patient's likelihood of developing a pressure ulcer – localised skin/soft-tissue injury over a bony prominence caused by pressure, shear, or friction, often compounded by immobility, poor nutrition, moisture, and altered sensation. It does NOT measure an existing ulcer; it directs preventive care.
Waterlow: higher total = higher risk (UK-common).
Braden: lower total = higher risk (6 subscales, opposite direction).
2Components – Waterlow risk factors
Waterlow sums points across baseline categories plus weighted special-risk categories:
⚖️Build / BMI
Weight for height – obese and, especially, cachectic/underweight both add points
🩹Skin type / risk areas
Visual skin condition – dry, oedematous, clammy, discoloured, broken
🚻Sex & age
Female and increasing age score higher
💧Continence
Incontinence of urine/faeces, or catheterised – moisture damage
🚶Mobility
Restless, apathetic, restricted, bedbound/chairbound – more immobile scores higher
🍽️Appetite / weight loss
Poor intake, anorexia, recent unplanned weight loss
📉Tissue malnutrition
Special risk – cachexia, organ failure, peripheral vascular disease, anaemia
🧠Neurological deficit
Special risk – diabetes, stroke, MS, sensory/motor loss
🔪Major surgery / trauma
Special risk – orthopaedic/spinal, prolonged operating time, on table
💊Medication
Special risk – high-dose steroids, cytotoxics, anti-inflammatories
The Braden scale instead scores 6 subscales – sensory perception, moisture, activity, mobility, nutrition, and friction/shear – each 1–4 (friction/shear 1–3), totalling 6–23.
3Scoring & thresholds
Note the two scales move in OPPOSITE directions.
Waterlow ≥10→At risk
Waterlow ≥15→High risk
Waterlow ≥20→Very high risk
Braden 19–23→Low / no risk
Braden 15–18→Mild risk
Braden 13–14→Moderate risk
Braden 10–12→High risk
Braden ≤9→Very high risk
4Prevention & grading of established ulcers
Any at-risk patient should receive the SSKIN prevention bundle:
Surface – pressure-redistributing mattress/cushion.
Skin inspection – regular assessment of high-risk areas.
Keep moving – repositioning, e.g. 2-hourly turns.
Incontinence / moisture management.
Nutrition & hydration optimisation.
Existing ulcers are graded by the EPUAP/NPUAP categories 1–4:
1️⃣Category 1
Non-blanching erythema of intact skin
2️⃣Category 2
Partial-thickness skin loss or intact/ruptured blister
3️⃣Category 3
Full-thickness skin loss – subcutaneous fat visible
4️⃣Category 4
Full-thickness tissue loss – muscle, tendon, or bone exposed
Additional descriptors: unstageable (base obscured by slough/eschar) and deep tissue injury (persistent non-blanching deep red/maroon/purple discolouration). Common sites: sacrum, heels, ischial tuberosities, and greater trochanter.
🚩 Pressure ulcers are largely PREVENTABLE and are treated as a marker of care quality (category 3–4 are reportable harms). No score replaces clinical judgement – reassess risk regularly and after any change in condition. Category 3–4 ulcers need specialist wound care/tissue viability review. Remember the trap: a LOW Braden = HIGH risk, opposite to Waterlow.
🎓 Directions are the classic exam catch: Waterlow HIGH = high risk (≥10 at risk, ≥15 high, ≥20 very high); Braden LOW = high risk (≤9 very high). Prevention is the SSKIN bundle: Surface, Skin inspection, Keep moving, Incontinence/moisture, Nutrition.

The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is the standard tool for assessing and communicating a patient's level of consciousness. It sums three components — Eye opening, Verbal response and Motor response — for a total between 3 (deep coma) and 15 (fully alert). Its power is in serial measurement: a falling GCS flags a deteriorating brain and drives urgent escalation.

1When to use it
Use the GCS in head injury / trauma, and for reduced consciousness of any cause (stroke, sepsis, metabolic, poisoning, post-ictal). Its greatest value is serial monitoring to detect deterioration early. Always assess pupils (size, symmetry, reactivity) and lateralising signs alongside it. For a rapid bedside screen use AVPU — Alert, responds to Voice, responds to Pain, Unresponsive — where “P” corresponds roughly to a GCS of 8.
2The three components (E + V + M)
👁️EYE opening (E, /4)
4 spontaneous · 3 to speech/sound · 2 to pain/pressure · 1 none
💬VERBAL response (V, /5)
5 orientated · 4 confused · 3 inappropriate words · 2 incomprehensible sounds · 1 none
💪MOTOR response (M, /6)
6 obeys commands · 5 localises to pain · 4 normal flexion (withdraws) · 3 abnormal flexion (decorticate) · 2 extension (decerebrate) · 1 none

Always report the breakdown, not just the total — e.g. E3V4M5 = 12. The motor score is the most prognostically important component.

3Scoring & thresholds
13–15→Mild brain injury / impairment
9–12→Moderate brain injury
≤8→Severe brain injury — comatose; cannot protect airway → consider intubation (“GCS 8, intubate”)
Drop ≥2 points→Significant deterioration — urgent senior review + CT head
4Interpretation & confounders
A single number is only a snapshot — the trend matters most; document E, V and M separately every time.
Several factors confound the score: intoxication/alcohol, sedation, and dysphasia (falsely low verbal).
In an intubated patient the verbal component cannot be tested — record it as Vₖ (T) for “tube” rather than guessing a number.
🚩 GCS ≤8 = at risk of airway compromise. The patient can no longer reliably protect their airway — call for urgent anaesthetic / airway support and consider intubation. A fall of ≥2 points is significant deterioration warranting urgent senior review and CT head. Always document E, V and M separately, and record confounders (intoxication, sedation, dysphasia, intubation).
🎓 The motor response is the single most prognostically important component. Remember the classic exam rule — “GCS 8 = intubate” — and always report the full breakdown (E_V_M_), never just the total.

The Apfel score is a simple bedside tool that predicts the risk of post-operative nausea and vomiting (PONV) in adults undergoing general anaesthesia. It uses four independent, equally-weighted risk factors (each worth 1 point, maximum 4) to stratify risk and guide how aggressively antiemetic prophylaxis is given. It does not diagnose PONV — it estimates the pre-operative probability so the anaesthetic technique and prophylaxis can be tailored.

1WHEN TO USE IT
Applied pre-operatively in adults planned for general anaesthesia to estimate the baseline probability of PONV within 24 hours of surgery. PONV is one of the commonest and most distressing complications of anaesthesia — a leading cause of patient dissatisfaction, unplanned admission and delayed discharge from day-surgery. The score turns four easy yes/no questions into a risk band that determines the number of antiemetic interventions offered.
2THE FOUR RISK FACTORS
Each factor scores exactly 1 point. They are independent and equally weighted.
♀️FEMALE SEX
+1 point — the single strongest predictor
🚭NON-SMOKER
+1 point — smokers are paradoxically protected
🤢PRIOR PONV / MOTION SICKNESS
+1 point — history of PONV or motion sickness
💊POST-OP OPIOIDS
+1 point — anticipated post-operative opioid use
Sum the points present (0–4) to obtain the Apfel score.
All four factors carry equal weight — there is no multiplier.
3SCORE → PREDICTED RISK & PROPHYLAXIS
Each additional point roughly doubles the early risk; risk climbs in ~20% steps.
0 points→~10% risk — low; often no routine prophylaxis needed
1 point→~20% risk — low–moderate; consider single agent
2 points→~40% risk — moderate; give 1–2 antiemetics from different classes
3 points→~60% risk — high; combination prophylaxis + modify technique
4 points→~80% risk — very high; multimodal prophylaxis + TIVA, minimise opioids
4MANAGEMENT & PROPHYLAXIS STRATEGY
A higher score prompts more interventions: first reduce baseline risk, then layer antiemetics from different receptor classes.
Reduce baseline risk: use regional anaesthesia where feasible, avoid volatile agents and nitrous oxide, favour propofol TIVA, minimise opioids (multimodal/opioid-sparing analgesia) and ensure adequate hydration.
5-HT₃ antagonist: ondansetron.
Corticosteroid: dexamethasone (given at induction).
Antihistamine: cyclizine.
Dopamine (D₂) antagonist: prochlorperazine or droperidol.
NK₁ antagonist: consider aprepitant in the highest-risk cases.
Combine agents from different classes for higher-risk patients — targeting multiple receptors is more effective than doubling one class.
🚩 PONV is a leading cause of patient dissatisfaction and delayed discharge. For higher-risk patients give combination antiemetics from different classes — not repeated doses of one. Watch drug side-effects: QT prolongation with ondansetron and droperidol, and extrapyramidal effects with dopamine antagonists (prochlorperazine, droperidol, metoclopramide).
🎓 Mnemonic — the four Apfel factors: Female, non-smoker, prior PONV / motion sickness, and post-op opioids. Each adds +1, and predicted risk rises roughly 10 / 20 / 40 / 60 / 80% for scores 0 → 4.

The ASA Physical Status classification is a pre-operative grading of a patient's baseline systemic health and fitness for anaesthesia, devised by the American Society of Anesthesiologists. It runs from ASA I (a normal, healthy patient) to ASA VI (a declared brain-dead organ donor), providing a shorthand for perioperative communication and a broad correlate of perioperative risk. It grades the patient, not the operation — it does not by itself account for the type or urgency of surgery, nor airway difficulty.

1What it is & when it is used
Assigned at the pre-operative assessment for every patient undergoing anaesthesia (surgical or procedural). Its purpose is standardised communication of a patient's baseline physiological reserve between clinicians. It correlates with — but does not solely determine — perioperative morbidity and mortality, length of stay and unplanned ICU admission. It is a global clinical judgement, not a calculated score.
2The six grades
💚ASA I
Normal healthy patient — non-smoker, no or minimal alcohol
🚬ASA II
Mild systemic disease, no functional limitation — smoker, social alcohol, pregnancy, BMI 30–40, well-controlled DM/HTN, mild lung disease
⚠️ASA III
Severe systemic disease with substantive functional limitation — poorly-controlled DM/HTN, COPD, BMI ≥40, alcohol dependence, pacemaker, reduced EF, ESRD on dialysis, MI/CVA/TIA/stent >3 months ago
🔥ASA IV
Severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life — recent (<3 months) MI/CVA/TIA/stent, ongoing ischaemia, severe valve dysfunction, sepsis, DIC, ESRD not on dialysis
🆘ASA V
Moribund patient not expected to survive without the operation — ruptured AAA, massive trauma, intracranial bleed with mass effect
🕊️ASA VI
Declared brain-dead patient whose organs are being removed for donation
3Grade → worked example
ASA I→Fit 25-year-old for elective knee arthroscopy
ASA II→Well-controlled type 2 diabetic, current smoker; or an uncomplicated pregnancy
ASA III→COPD on home O₂, BMI 45, dialysis-dependent — substantive limitation
ASA IV→MI 6 weeks ago with ongoing angina, or septic shock
ASA V→Ruptured AAA in extremis — surgery is the only chance of survival
ASA VI→Brain-stem-death-confirmed donor in theatre for organ retrieval
4The 'E' suffix & interpretation
An E is appended for Emergency surgery — a procedure where delay would significantly increase the threat to life or a body part (e.g. ASA IIIE, ASA VE). Emergency status independently raises perioperative risk.
Grade reflects baseline physical status only — it is deliberately independent of the planned operation.
Higher grades track with rising mortality, but ASA alone is a blunt tool — combine with surgical severity, functional capacity and frailty.
🚩 ASA is subjective and grades baseline patient fitness only — it ignores the surgery type, airway difficulty and urgency in isolation. Never use it as a standalone predictor: integrate it with surgical risk, functional capacity (METs), frailty scores and investigations. The 'E' suffix (emergency) denotes a substantially higher-risk case and must not be omitted.
What to do with a high grade: ASA III+ or an emergency (“E”) case → early senior anaesthetic review, preoperative optimisation of comorbidities, and consider HDU/ITU booking and prehabilitation — read alongside surgical severity, METs and frailty. Pre-operative assessment ›
🎓 Memory hook — I healthy · II mild disease (no limitation) · III severe disease with functional limitation · IV severe disease that is a constant threat to life · V moribund, won't survive without the op · VI brain-dead organ donor. Add E for emergency.

The WHO Analgesic Ladder is a stepwise framework for titrating pain relief according to severity. Devised in 1986 for cancer pain, it is now applied widely to acute and chronic pain. Its governing principle is to match the strength of analgesia to the intensity of pain, moving up the ladder if pain persists or worsens and down as it settles — delivered by the mouth, by the clock, by the ladder.

1How to use it — the three principles
By the mouth — use the oral route wherever possible; it is simple, effective and acceptable to patients.
By the clock — give analgesia at regular fixed intervals, not only PRN, so pain is prevented rather than chased.
By the ladder — start at the step appropriate to severity; escalate if pain is uncontrolled and de-escalate as it improves.
Adjuvants (co-analgesics) may be added at any step. Always reassess response and titrate.
2The three steps (± adjuvant)
💊STEP 1 — Mild pain
Non-opioid ± adjuvant: paracetamol and/or an NSAID
💊STEP 2 — Moderate pain
Weak opioid + non-opioid ± adjuvant: codeine, dihydrocodeine, tramadol
💉STEP 3 — Severe pain
Strong opioid + non-opioid ± adjuvant: morphine (1st-line), oxycodone, fentanyl, buprenorphine
🧩ADJUVANTS — any step
Neuropathic: amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin, pregabalin; also corticosteroids, bisphosphonates (bone pain), antispasmodics
3Step → drugs (what to reach for)
Step 1→Paracetamol 1 g QDS and/or NSAID (e.g. ibuprofen, naproxen); add adjuvant if neuropathic
Step 2→Codeine / dihydrocodeine / tramadol, added to step 1 agents (do not stop the non-opioid)
Step 3→Morphine first-line; oxycodone / fentanyl / buprenorphine as alternatives, added to step 1 agents
Any step→Adjuvant for neuropathic pain (amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin, pregabalin) or bone/spasm pain
4Safe opioid prescribing
Regular + PRN — prescribe a regular background dose plus a breakthrough (PRN) dose of roughly 1/6 of the total 24-hour dose.
Anticipate side effects — co-prescribe a laxative for constipation (near-universal, does not wane) and an antiemetic for early nausea.
Monitor — watch for sedation, respiratory depression, tolerance and dependence; review efficacy and dose regularly.
Reversal — naloxone reverses opioid toxicity (titrate to respiratory rate, not full alertness, in dependence/palliative settings).
🚩 Opioids: co-prescribe a laxative and monitor for toxicity — the triad of pinpoint pupils + drowsiness + low respiratory rate signals overdose → give naloxone. In renal impairment avoid morphine (active metabolites accumulate causing sedation/myoclonus) — prefer oxycodone, alfentanil or buprenorphine. NSAIDs are cautioned in renal impairment, GI ulcer/bleed risk, cardiovascular disease and asthma.
🎓 Remember the three ‘by’s: by the mouth, by the clock, by the ladder. Breakthrough dose ≈ 1/6 of the 24-hour dose. Adjuvants for neuropathic pain can be added at any step — and when escalating a step you add to, not replace, the non-opioid.

AEIOU is the classic mnemonic for the emergency (acute) indications for renal replacement therapy (RRT) in acute kidney injury (AKI). It is not a numerical risk score but a decision aid: AKI is first managed medically, and RRT — usually haemodialysis or haemofiltration — is indicated when one of five life-threatening complications becomes refractory to that medical treatment. AEIOU = Acidosis, Electrolytes (hyperkalaemia), Intoxication, Overload, Uraemia.

1WHEN TO USE IT — MEDICAL MANAGEMENT FIRST

AEIOU identifies the point at which AKI can no longer be managed conservatively. Every patient with AKI is first treated medically: identify and treat the cause, optimise fluid balance and renal perfusion, stop nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, aminoglycosides, contrast), and actively manage hyperkalaemia and acidosis. RRT is escalated to only when one of the five indications persists despite maximal medical therapy — the recurring theme is that each indication is an emergency because it is refractory.

Not every AKI needs dialysis — most recover with supportive care.
RRT buys time and corrects the immediate threat while the kidneys recover or the cause is treated.
2THE FIVE INDICATIONS — AEIOU
🧪A — ACIDOSIS
Severe metabolic acidosis, e.g. pH <7.1–7.2, refractory to medical treatment (fluids, treating cause; consider bicarbonate).
⚡E — ELECTROLYTES
Refractory hyperkalaemia — K⁺ >6.5 (or >7) or with ECG changes, not responding to medical management.
☠️I — INTOXICATION
Dialysable toxins/drugs (BLAST): Barbiturates, Lithium, Alcohols (methanol, ethylene glycol), Salicylates/aspirin, Theophylline; also metformin (lactic acidosis).
💧O — OVERLOAD
Refractory fluid/volume overload — pulmonary oedema unresponsive to diuretics.
🧠U — URAEMIA
Symptomatic/severe uraemia — encephalopathy, pericarditis (rub), uraemic bleeding, or very high urea.
3THRESHOLDS & ACTIONS
pH <7.1–7.2, refractory→Acidosis indication — RRT to correct severe metabolic acidosis
K⁺ >6.5 / >7 or ECG changes, refractory→Emergency RRT for hyperkalaemia after medical measures fail
Dialysable toxin (BLAST + metformin)→Haemodialysis to remove the poison — discuss with toxicology/renal
Pulmonary oedema unresponsive to diuretics→RRT for fluid removal (ultrafiltration)
Uraemic encephalopathy / pericarditis / bleeding→Urgent RRT — these are true emergency indications
4MODALITIES & CLINICAL USE

Choice of modality depends on the patient's haemodynamic stability and the setting.

Intermittent haemodialysis (IHD) — rapid solute/fluid clearance; suits the haemodynamically stable ward patient.
Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT / haemofiltration) — slower, gentler; preferred for haemodynamically unstable ITU patients.
Peritoneal dialysis — uses the peritoneum as the membrane; less common for acute adult AKI in the UK.

AEIOU is a clinical trigger, not a substitute for judgement: decisions are individualised and made with early involvement of renal and critical care teams.

🚩 These are indications only when refractory to medical management. Treat hyperkalaemia first — calcium gluconate to protect the myocardium, then insulin–dextrose and nebulised salbutamol — and correct acidosis before escalating. Uraemic pericarditis and uraemic encephalopathy are urgent indications for RRT. Refer to renal/critical care early rather than waiting for the patient to deteriorate.
🎓 AEIOU = Acidosis, Electrolytes (hyperkalaemia), Intoxication, Overload, Uraemia — start RRT when medical management fails.

The International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) is a validated, self-administered questionnaire that quantifies the severity of lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS), most often in men with benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). Seven symptom questions are each scored 0–5 (from ‘not at all’ to ‘almost always’), giving a total of 0–35. A separate eighth question rates the quality-of-life (‘bother’) impact on a 0–6 scale. The score does not diagnose BPH — it grades symptom burden, guides management and tracks treatment response.

1When to use it & what it measures
Use the IPSS to quantify LUTS severity at baseline in men presenting with urinary symptoms (typically suspected BPH), to guide management and to monitor response to treatment or watchful waiting. It is symptom-based and subjective — it reflects how bothersome symptoms are, not prostate size or bladder outflow physiology. Always pair it with the QoL question: a modest score with high bother may still warrant treatment.
Storage / irritative: frequency, urgency, nocturia
Voiding / obstructive: weak stream, straining, intermittency, incomplete emptying
2The seven symptom domains
Each question below is scored 0–5. Storage symptoms cluster together, as do voiding symptoms — a useful way to characterise the predominant problem and steer treatment choice.
💧Frequency
Storage — passing urine <2h apart (0–5)
⚡Urgency
Storage — difficulty postponing (0–5)
🌙Nocturia
Storage — times waking to void (0–5)
🚿Weak stream
Voiding — reduced flow force (0–5)
💪Straining
Voiding — pushing to start/maintain (0–5)
〰️Intermittency
Voiding — stopping/starting stream (0–5)
🩹Incomplete emptying
Voiding — sensation of residual urine (0–5)

A separate 8th question asks: “If you had to spend the rest of your life with your urinary condition as it is now, how would you feel?” — scored 0 (delighted) to 6 (terrible). This QoL/bother score is reported alongside the total but is not added to it.

3Scoring & severity bands
Sum the seven symptom questions for a total of 0–35 and read off the severity band. Bands guide the intensity of management and set a baseline against which to measure treatment response.
0–7→Mild — watchful waiting, conservative measures
8–19→Moderate — consider medical therapy (guided by bother)
20–35→Severe — medical therapy; consider surgery if refractory
Surgery = TURP first-line; a very large gland or refractory retention → open or laser (HoLEP) prostatectomy. Classic complication: TURP syndrome (dilutional hyponatraemia/fluid overload from glycine irrigation absorption). Benign prostatic hyperplasia ›
4Management & workup of BPH LUTS
Assessment first: examination including DRE, urinalysis (exclude infection/haematuria), PSA (with counselling), post-void residual and flow rate. Then manage by severity and bother:
Conservative: fluid advice (reduce evening/caffeine/alcohol intake), bladder training, reassurance — for mild symptoms or low bother.
Alpha-blocker (e.g. tamsulosin): relaxes prostatic smooth muscle for rapid symptom relief; caution with postural hypotension/dizziness and floppy iris in cataract surgery.
5-alpha-reductase inhibitor (e.g. finasteride): shrinks the prostate over months, best for larger glands; note it lowers PSA (roughly halves it) and reduces long-term retention/surgery risk.
Storage-predominant symptoms: add an anticholinergic or mirabegron for overactive-bladder features.
Surgery (TURP): for refractory, complicated or severe disease (recurrent retention, stones, renal impairment, recurrent UTI or haematuria).
🚩 The IPSS grades symptoms — it does not exclude serious pathology. Actively look for red flags: haematuria, recurrent UTI, palpable bladder / retention, renal impairment and an abnormal (hard/nodular) DRE — the latter warrants a 2-week-wait referral for suspected prostate cancer. Rule out UTI before attributing symptoms to BPH. Acute urinary retention is a urological emergency — catheterise.
🎓 High-yield: 7 symptom questions, each 0–5 (total 0–35) plus 1 separate QoL/bother question 0–6. Bands: 0–7 mild, 8–19 moderate, 20–35 severe. Classify symptoms as storage (frequency, urgency, nocturia) vs voiding (weak stream, straining, intermittency, incomplete emptying) — it steers treatment choice.

The Bosniak classification stratifies cystic renal masses on contrast-enhanced CT (or MRI) into five categories that estimate the probability of malignancy and dictate management. The single most important discriminator is enhancement — measurable uptake of contrast within walls, septa or solid components indicates vascularity and drives a lesion into a higher category. It converts a subjective ‘this cyst looks complex’ into a reproducible risk band linked to a clear action: reassure, follow up, or resect.

1When to use it & what it estimates

Apply Bosniak when a renal cyst is not a simple cyst on cross-sectional imaging, or as a framework for any incidentally detected cystic renal lesion. It requires a dedicated contrast-enhanced study with pre- and post-contrast phases so enhancement can be objectively assessed (a rise of ≥15 HU is generally taken as true enhancement). It estimates likelihood of malignancy and maps that risk onto management — no follow-up, surveillance imaging, or surgery.

Assess: wall thickness, number and thickness of septa, calcification, and — critically — enhancement.
Enhancing solid or soft-tissue components carry the highest malignant risk.
2The categories
💧I
Simple benign cyst: thin hairline wall, no septa/calcification/solid components, no enhancement, water density. ~0% malignant.
🔹II
Minimally complex benign: a few thin septa, fine calcification, or a ≤3 cm hyperdense non-enhancing cyst. Benign.
🔍IIF
Follow-up: multiple thin septa, minimal smooth wall/septal thickening, or thicker/nodular calcification — all non-enhancing. ~5–10% malignant.
⚠️III
Indeterminate: thick/irregular walls or septa with MEASURABLE ENHANCEMENT. ~50% malignant.
🔴IV
Clearly malignant: enhancing SOFT-TISSUE/solid components adjacent to but independent of wall/septa. ~90%+ malignant.
3Category → malignancy risk → management
I — simple cyst (~0%)→Benign; no follow-up.
II — minimally complex (benign)→Benign; no follow-up.
IIF — follow-up (~5–10%)→Surveillance imaging; do NOT discharge.
III — enhancing walls/septa (~50%)→Surgical resection / partial nephrectomy (ablation or active surveillance in selected patients).
IV — enhancing solid component (~90%+)→Surgical resection.
4Interpretation & clinical use

Categories I and II are benign and need no follow-up. IIF (the ‘F’ is for follow-up) is deliberately hedged — its features are probably benign but not certainly so, hence interval surveillance imaging to confirm stability. III and IV both enhance and are treated surgically, differing in whether the enhancing tissue is in the wall/septa (III) or forms a discrete solid nodule (IV).

The line between IIF and III is enhancement: non-enhancing complexity is IIF; measurable enhancement is III.
Classification requires adequate contrast technique — a poor study can under- or over-call a lesion.
🚩 Enhancement is the critical feature — measurable contrast uptake pushes a lesion into category III or IV and mandates surgical resection. Never discharge a category IIF lesion: it requires follow-up imaging. If malignancy is suspected, correlate with full renal cell carcinoma work-up, including staging CT of chest/abdomen/pelvis. Most renal cancers are clear cell RCC.
🎓 I & II benign → no follow-up; IIF → follow-up imaging; III (enhancing walls/septa, ~50%) and IV (enhancing solid components, ~90%) → surgery. Enhancement is the key to malignancy — if it enhances, think resection.

The IMDC (International Metastatic RCC Database Consortium) model — also called the Heng criteria — is a validated prognostic tool for metastatic renal cell carcinoma (mRCC). It uses six readily available clinical and laboratory factors, each worth 1 point, to stratify patients into favourable, intermediate or poor risk groups. This predicts median overall survival and helps guide selection of first-line systemic therapy.

1WHEN TO USE IT — METASTATIC RCC
RCC (most commonly clear cell) classically presents with the triad of haematuria, flank pain and a palpable mass, though most are now found incidentally on imaging. It can drive paraneoplastic features — polycythaemia (ectopic EPO), hypercalcaemia and Stauffer syndrome (non-metastatic hepatic dysfunction). Localised disease is treated with nephrectomy; once disease is metastatic, management shifts to systemic therapy ± cytoreductive nephrectomy. The IMDC model is applied at the point of starting first-line systemic therapy to prognosticate and stratify treatment.
2THE SIX RISK FACTORS (1 POINT EACH)
🏃PERFORMANCE STATUS
Karnofsky performance status < 80%
⏱️TIME TO TREATMENT
< 1 year from diagnosis to systemic therapy
🩸ANAEMIA
Haemoglobin < lower limit of normal
🦴HYPERCALCAEMIA
Corrected calcium > upper limit of normal
⚪NEUTROPHILIA
Neutrophils > upper limit of normal
🩹THROMBOCYTOSIS
Platelets > upper limit of normal
3RISK GROUPS & SURVIVAL
0 factors — FAVOURABLE→Best prognosis; median overall survival ~43 months
1–2 factors — INTERMEDIATE→Median overall survival ~23 months
3–6 factors — POOR→Median overall survival ~8 months
4GUIDING SYSTEMIC THERAPY
Favourable risk: options include TKI monotherapy (sunitinib, pazopanib) or an immunotherapy–TKI combination such as axitinib + pembrolizumab.
Intermediate / poor risk: dual immune checkpoint blockade with ipilimumab + nivolumab is a key option, as are immunotherapy–TKI combinations.
RCC is relatively chemo- and radio-resistant, so treatment relies on immunotherapy and targeted (anti-VEGF / TKI) agents rather than conventional cytotoxic chemotherapy.
🚩 IMDC applies to metastatic RCC only — not localised disease (which is managed by nephrectomy). It is a tool for prognostication and systemic therapy selection, not for deciding surgery. Remember RCC is relatively chemo/radio-resistant: immunotherapy and targeted TKI/anti-VEGF therapies are the mainstays.
🎓 Six factors, 1 point each: performance status < 80%, < 1 year to treatment, anaemia, hypercalcaemia, neutrophilia, thrombocytosis. Scoring: 0 = favourable, 1–2 = intermediate, 3–6 = poor.
RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__Neurology:
Stroke is a clinical emergency where “time is brain”. Two scores dominate the acute pathway: ROSIER (Recognition of Stroke in the Emergency Room) helps confirm that a patient presenting to the ED is genuinely having a stroke, and the NIHSS (National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale) quantifies its severity to guide reperfusion decisions and monitor progress. Neither replaces urgent non-contrast CT to exclude haemorrhage, and both demand that hypoglycaemia — the great stroke mimic — is excluded first.

1WHERE EACH SCORE SITS IN THE PATHWAY
Community / prehospital: FAST (Face, Arm, Speech, Time) flags a suspected stroke and triggers a blue-light transfer.
ED assessment: ROSIER confirms whether this is likely a stroke rather than a mimic — but always check a capillary glucose first, as hypoglycaemia can reproduce focal deficits.
Severity & treatment: once stroke is confirmed and haemorrhage excluded on CT, NIHSS quantifies severity to guide thrombolysis / thrombectomy and to track the patient over time.
2ROSIER COMPONENTS

Score after excluding hypoglycaemia. Two features subtract a point (they point away from stroke), five add a point.

😵LOC / SYNCOPE
Loss of consciousness or syncope → −1
⚡SEIZURE
Seizure activity → −1
😐FACE
Asymmetric facial weakness → +1
💪ARM
Asymmetric arm weakness → +1
🦵LEG
Asymmetric leg weakness → +1
🗣️SPEECH
Speech disturbance → +1
👁️VISUAL FIELD
Visual field defect → +1
Total > 0→Stroke likely — activate stroke pathway, urgent CT
Total ≤ 0→Stroke unlikely, but does NOT exclude it — keep clinical suspicion high
3NIHSS — SEVERITY SCORE (0–42)

Eleven items scored on neurological examination, higher = more severe deficit.

Consciousness: level of consciousness + orientation questions + response to commands.
Cranial / visual: best gaze, visual fields, facial palsy.
Motor: motor arm (left & right), motor leg (left & right), limb ataxia.
Sensory & higher function: sensory, best language / aphasia, dysarthria, extinction & inattention (neglect).
0→No stroke symptoms
1–4→Minor stroke
5–15→Moderate stroke
16–20→Moderate–severe stroke
21–42→Severe stroke
4ACUTE ISCHAEMIC STROKE PATHWAY
Confirm & image: ROSIER positive → urgent non-contrast CT head to exclude haemorrhage before any treatment.
Thrombolysis: if ischaemic and within window, IV alteplase or tenecteplase within 4.5 hours of onset (no contraindication, haemorrhage excluded).
Thrombectomy: mechanical clot retrieval for large-vessel occlusion — up to 24 hours in selected patients with favourable imaging.
Antiplatelet: aspirin 300 mg once haemorrhage is excluded on CT, continued for 2 weeks then switched to long-term secondary prevention.
🚩 Always exclude HYPOGLYCAEMIA first — check a capillary glucose, as it is a classic stroke mimic. Time is brain: get urgent CT and involve the stroke team immediately. Do NOT give aspirin or thrombolysis until haemorrhage is excluded on CT.
🎓 ROSIER > 0 = stroke likely (assess in ED); NIHSS quantifies severity and guides thrombolysis / thrombectomy decisions; and whatever the score, exclude hypoglycaemia before you commit.

The McDonald Criteria are the internationally used diagnostic criteria for multiple sclerosis (MS). Rather than predicting risk, they establish a diagnosis by demonstrating that CNS demyelinating lesions are disseminated in SPACE (different locations) and in TIME (occurring at different times), while requiring that there is no better explanation for the clinical picture. The 2017 revision streamlined diagnosis, notably allowing CSF-specific oligoclonal bands to substitute for dissemination in time.

1WHEN TO USE & WHAT IT ESTABLISHES
Applied to a patient presenting with a typical clinical syndrome suggestive of CNS demyelination (e.g. optic neuritis, a brainstem/cerebellar syndrome, or a partial myelitis). The criteria integrate clinical attacks, MRI, and CSF findings to confirm MS. The higher the number of clinical attacks and objectively evidenced lesions, the less additional paraclinical evidence is needed.
An attack (relapse): patient-reported symptoms with objective findings lasting ≥ 24 hours, in the absence of fever or infection.
Two components must both be shown: dissemination in space (DIS) and dissemination in time (DIT).
2DISSEMINATION IN SPACE & TIME — THE CRITERIA
DIS = ≥ 1 T2 lesion in ≥ 2 of the 4 characteristic CNS areas. DIT = simultaneous gadolinium-enhancing and non-enhancing lesions, OR a new lesion on follow-up MRI, OR CSF-specific oligoclonal bands.
🧠PERIVENTRICULAR
DIS site 1 — T2 lesion adjacent to the ventricles
🧩(JUXTA)CORTICAL
DIS site 2 — cortical or juxtacortical T2 lesion
🧬INFRATENTORIAL
DIS site 3 — brainstem or cerebellar T2 lesion
🦴SPINAL CORD
DIS site 4 — T2 lesion in the spinal cord
⏱️ENHANCE MIX
DIT — simultaneous gadolinium-enhancing & non-enhancing lesions
🔁NEW LESION
DIT — new T2/enhancing lesion on follow-up MRI
🧪OLIGOCLONAL BANDS
DIT substitute — CSF-specific bands, absent in serum
3CLINICAL APPLICATION — ATTACKS & LESIONS
How much paraclinical evidence you need depends on how much the clinical picture already provides.
≥ 2 attacks + objective evidence of ≥ 2 lesions→MS diagnosed clinically — no further tests strictly required
≥ 2 attacks + objective evidence of 1 lesion→Need DIS (MRI or a further clinical attack in a different site)
1 attack + objective evidence of ≥ 2 lesions→Need DIT (MRI, or CSF oligoclonal bands substitute)
1 attack + 1 lesion (clinically isolated syndrome)→Need both DIS and DIT to confirm MS
DIS + DIT + ≥ 1 yr progression (no relapses)→Consider primary progressive MS pathway
4INVESTIGATIONS, TYPES & MIMICS
MRI brain + cord with gadolinium — the mainstay; demonstrates DIS and DIT.
CSF — oligoclonal bands present in CSF but not serum, indicating intrathecal IgG synthesis.
Visual evoked potentials — delayed conduction can provide supportive evidence of prior optic nerve demyelination.
Clinical types: relapsing-remitting (commonest), secondary progressive, and primary progressive. Always actively exclude mimics: NMOSD (aquaporin-4 antibody), MOG antibody disease, CNS vasculitis, and B₁₂ deficiency.
🚩 'No better explanation' is essential — the criteria are only valid once mimics are excluded. NMOSD (aquaporin-4 antibody) is a critical differential requiring different treatment and can be worsened by some MS therapies. Note that CSF-specific oligoclonal bands can now fulfil DIT in the 2017 revision — but they are not fully specific to MS and must be interpreted in context.
Once MS is confirmed → refer to neurology to start a disease-modifying therapy (DMT); treat acute relapses with steroids and manage symptoms (spasticity, bladder, fatigue). Multiple sclerosis ›
🎓 MS = lesions disseminated in SPACE and TIME. The 4 DIS sites are periventricular, (juxta)cortical, infratentorial, and spinal cord. In the 2017 revision, CSF oligoclonal bands substitute for DIT — a very high-yield exam point.

The El Escorial criteria (and their Awaji modification) are the standardised diagnostic frameworks for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) / motor neurone disease (MND). They do not generate a numerical score; instead they grade diagnostic certainty by requiring evidence of both upper motor neurone (UMN) and lower motor neurone (LMN) dysfunction, progressive spread of signs, and exclusion of mimics. Certainty rises with the number of CNS regions involved.

1When to use it & the core rule
Apply in an adult with progressive, painless weakness where MND is suspected. Diagnosis rests on a triad: (1) UMN signs, (2) LMN signs, and (3) progressive spread of symptoms/signs within a region or to other regions, with exclusion of other causes. Crucially there is NO sensory involvement, and sphincter function, eye movements and cognition (largely) are typically spared — features that help separate MND from mimics.
2The four CNS regions & the signs to elicit
Certainty is built region-by-region. Each of the four regions is assessed for UMN and LMN signs.
🗣️Bulbar
dysarthria, dysphagia, tongue wasting/fasciculation, brisk jaw jerk, pseudobulbar affect
💪Cervical
upper-limb wasting/fasciculation + brisk reflexes / spasticity
🫁Thoracic
paraspinal/abdominal wall involvement; declining respiratory (FVC) function
🦵Lumbosacral
lower-limb wasting/fasciculation + upgoing plantars, brisk reflexes, spasticity
UMN signs: spasticity, brisk/pathologically preserved reflexes, upgoing plantars (Babinski), pseudobulbar affect.
LMN signs: muscle wasting, fasciculations, weakness, hypotonia, hyporeflexia.
3El Escorial certainty categories (by number of regions)
The revised El Escorial criteria grade certainty by how many of the four regions show combined UMN + LMN involvement.
UMN + LMN in ≥3 regions→Clinically Definite ALS
≥2 regions, UMN signs rostral to LMN signs→Clinically Probable ALS
UMN in ≥1 region + EMG (LMN) evidence in ≥2 regions→Clinically Probable, lab-supported
UMN + LMN signs in only 1 region→Clinically Possible ALS
4Awaji modification, investigations & management
The Awaji criteria give electrophysiological (EMG) evidence of LMN dysfunction — fibrillations, fasciculation potentials and chronic neurogenic (reinnervation) changes — equal weight to clinical LMN signs. This improves early and sensitive diagnosis, letting subclinical denervation count toward a region.
Investigations: EMG/nerve conduction studies (active + chronic denervation, fasciculations, normal sensory conduction); MRI brain/spine to exclude structural mimic; bloods (including CK, exclude metabolic/inflammatory causes).
Exclude mimics: cervical spondylotic myelopathy, multifocal motor neuropathy (MMN — treatable), myasthenia gravis.
Management: multidisciplinary team; riluzole (modest survival benefit); non-invasive ventilation for respiratory failure; PEG for unsafe swallow; symptom control (secretions, spasticity, cramps). Prognosis is poor (~2–4 years, death usually from respiratory failure).
🚩 There is no cure — riluzole only modestly prolongs survival. Respiratory failure is the usual cause of death: monitor FVC and offer NIV early. Always exclude treatable mimics (especially cervical myelopathy and multifocal motor neuropathy) before confirming the diagnosis — criteria assume mimics have been ruled out.
🎓 ALS = mixed UMN + LMN signs with NO sensory loss. El Escorial grades certainty by the number of CNS regions involved; Awaji gives EMG equal weight to clinical LMN signs, enabling earlier diagnosis.

The House-Brackmann (HB) scale is the standard clinician-graded system for describing the severity of facial nerve (CN VII) palsy, most often applied to Bell's palsy — acute idiopathic lower motor neurone (LMN) facial weakness. It runs from Grade I (normal) to Grade VI (total paralysis) and is used both at presentation and to track recovery over weeks to months.

1When to use it & the LMN vs UMN rule
Use HB grading in any unilateral facial weakness to document baseline severity and monitor recovery. The critical first step is to localise the lesion. Bell's palsy is an LMN lesion affecting the whole half of the face — including the forehead. A central (UMN) lesion such as a stroke spares the forehead, because the upper face receives bilateral cortical innervation.
LMN (Bell's): forehead involved — cannot wrinkle/raise brow on affected side.
UMN (central): forehead spared — brow wrinkling preserved; think stroke → assess urgently.
Typical Bell's features: unilateral facial droop, inability to close the eye, loss of the nasolabial fold, and sometimes hyperacusis, altered taste (chorda tympani) and post-auricular pain.
2The six grades
