Each grade integrates resting symmetry, movement, eye closure and any synkinesis/contracture. Note the pivotal shift at Grade IV, where eye closure becomes incomplete.
✅Grade I — Normal
Normal facial function in all areas.
🙂Grade II — Mild
Slight weakness on close inspection; complete eye closure with minimal effort; slight asymmetry on movement.
😐Grade III — Moderate
Obvious but not disfiguring asymmetry; complete eye closure with effort; noticeable but not severe synkinesis/contracture.
😟Grade IV — Mod. severe
Obvious disfiguring weakness; incomplete eye closure; asymmetry at rest.
😣Grade V — Severe
Barely perceptible motion; incomplete eye closure; asymmetric at rest.
🚫Grade VI — Total
Total paralysis — no movement.
3Grade → clinical picture
Grade I–II→Normal / mild — good prognosis, eye closes fully.
Grade III→Moderate weakness but eye still closes with effort — cornea protected.
Grade IV–VI→Incomplete eye closure — mandates active eye protection to prevent exposure keratopathy.
Grade VI→Complete paralysis — poorest prognosis; reassess diagnosis and cause.
4Management of Bell's palsy
Steroids: oral corticosteroids (prednisolone) started within 72 hours of onset improve the chance of full recovery.
Eye protection (crucial): lubricating drops by day, ointment and taping the eye closed at night — incomplete closure risks exposure keratopathy and corneal ulceration.
Ramsay Hunt: if vesicles in the ear canal/auricle or severe pain — add antivirals (VZV reactivation).
Prognosis: most patients recover over weeks to months; HB grade is used to track improvement.
🚩 Forehead SPARING points to an UMN/central cause (e.g. stroke) — not Bell's — assess urgently. Any grade with incomplete eye closure (IV–VI) needs active eye protection to prevent exposure keratopathy/corneal ulcer. Consider Ramsay Hunt (VZV) and other secondary causes; bilateral or atypical palsy warrants investigation (Lyme disease, sarcoidosis, tumour).
🎓 Bell's = LMN palsy so the forehead is affected; a UMN lesion spares the forehead. Treat with prednisolone within 72h + eye protection. House-Brackmann runs I (normal) → VI (total paralysis), with incomplete eye closure appearing at Grade IV.

The ASIA Impairment Scale (AIS), from the American Spinal Injury Association, is the international standard for the neurological classification of traumatic spinal cord injury (ISNCSCI). A structured motor and sensory examination answers three questions: (1) the neurological level of injury (NLI) — the most caudal segment with normal motor and sensory function bilaterally; (2) whether the injury is complete or incomplete — decided entirely by sacral sparing; and (3) the AIS grade (A–E), which quantifies severity and guides prognosis.

1WHEN TO USE IT — the standardised SCI exam
Applied to any patient with confirmed or suspected traumatic spinal cord injury, after initial ABCDE assessment and spinal immobilisation. It provides a reproducible, common language for documenting deficit, tracking recovery, and prognosticating. The examination has two arms — motor (10 key muscles per side, graded 0–5 on the MRC scale) and sensory (28 dermatomes per side, tested for light touch and pinprick, scored 0–2) — plus a mandatory rectal (PR) examination for sacral function. Best performed once spinal shock (transient areflexia, which can mimic a complete injury) has been accounted for; serial exams matter.
2THE COMPONENTS — motor, sensory & the sacral check
Motor: 5 upper-limb key muscles (C5 elbow flexors → T1 finger abductors) and 5 lower-limb key muscles (L2 hip flexors → S1 ankle plantarflexors), each graded 0–5, per side (max 100).
Sensory: C2 down to S4–5, light touch and pinprick, each dermatome scored 0 (absent), 1 (altered), or 2 (normal), per side.
The decisive step — sacral sparing at S4–5: perianal light touch/pinprick, deep anal pressure (DAP), and voluntary anal contraction (VAC) on PR.
💪MOTOR
10 key muscles/side, MRC 0–5
✋LIGHT TOUCH
28 dermatomes/side, 0–2 (dorsal columns)
📌PINPRICK
28 dermatomes/side, 0–2 (spinothalamic)
🔑SACRAL SPARING
S4–5 sensation, DAP, VAC on PR — decides complete vs incomplete
3THE AIS GRADES — A to E
🅰️A — COMPLETE
No motor or sensory function in S4–5 (no sacral sparing)
🅱️B — SENSORY INCOMPLETE
Sensory (incl. S4–5) but no motor function below the NLI
🇨C — MOTOR INCOMPLETE
Motor preserved below NLI; >half of key muscles below power <3/5
🇩D — MOTOR INCOMPLETE
Motor preserved below NLI; ≥half of key muscles below power ≥3/5
🇪E — NORMAL
Normal motor & sensory in a patient with prior deficit
4INTERPRETATION & the incomplete cord syndromes
No sacral sparing (no S4–5 sensation, no DAP, no VAC)→COMPLETE injury = AIS A — poorest recovery potential
Any sacral sparing present→INCOMPLETE injury (AIS B–D) — better prognosis for recovery
Sacral sensory sparing but no motor below NLI→AIS B
Motor incomplete, majority of muscles below NLI ≥3/5→AIS D — often ambulatory potential
Central cord: hyperextension in elderly with cervical spondylosis — arms worse than legs; commonest incomplete syndrome.
Anterior cord: loss of motor + pain/temperature, dorsal columns (proprioception/vibration) spared — worst prognosis.
Brown-Séquard (hemisection): ipsilateral motor + dorsal-column loss, contralateral pain/temperature loss.
Posterior cord: loss of proprioception/vibration (rare). Conus medullaris / cauda equina: mixed LMN/UMN, bladder-bowel and saddle involvement.

Context: maintain immobilisation, ABCDE, urgent MRI to define cord/ligamentous injury, and early specialist (spinal) referral. Distinguish neurogenic shock (hypotension + bradycardia from sympathetic disruption) from spinal shock (transient areflexia). High-dose steroids are controversial and not routinely recommended.

🚩 Always assess SACRAL SPARING with a PR exam (perianal sensation, anal tone/squeeze, deep anal pressure) — it is the single finding that separates complete from incomplete injury and therefore prognosis; a spuriously "complete" picture may just be spinal shock. Do not confuse neurogenic shock (hypotension WITH bradycardia) with hypovolaemia. Cauda equina syndrome (bilateral sciatica, saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction) is a surgical emergency — immobilise, image, and refer early.
🎓 Run the ladder A → E: A = complete (no sacral sparing) → B sensory incomplete → C/D motor incomplete (split on the ≥3/5 majority rule) → E normal. Sacral sparing = incomplete = better prognosis. And know the incomplete cord syndromes: central (arms>legs, elderly), anterior (worst outcome), Brown-Séquard (hemisection).

The Modified Dandy criteria are the diagnostic criteria for idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH), also called pseudotumor cerebri or benign intracranial hypertension. IIH is raised intracranial pressure with no identifiable cause and, crucially, normal brain imaging. It classically affects young, obese women of childbearing age, and its principal danger is progressive, potentially permanent vision loss from chronic papilloedema. All five criteria must be satisfied to make the diagnosis.

1When to suspect it & who gets it
Suspect IIH in a patient with symptoms of raised ICP but a normal conscious level and normal scan. The classic patient is a young, obese woman of childbearing age. Known associations and precipitants include tetracyclines/doxycycline, vitamin A and retinoids (isotretinoin), oral contraceptives, and corticosteroids or steroid withdrawal. Presenting features include headache, transient visual obscurations, pulsatile tinnitus, nausea, and papilloedema on fundoscopy.
2The five modified Dandy criteria (ALL required)
🧠Raised ICP symptoms
Signs/symptoms of raised ICP: headache, papilloedema, transient visual obscurations, pulsatile tinnitus, nausea
👁️No localising signs*
No focal neurology EXCEPT a sixth (abducens) nerve palsy — a false localising sign of raised ICP
💧Raised CSF pressure
High LP opening pressure (>25 cm CSF / >250 mm) with NORMAL CSF composition
🖥️Normal imaging
No hydrocephalus, mass, or structural/vascular lesion; must EXCLUDE cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (MR/CT venography)
✅No other cause
Patient awake and alert; no other identified cause of raised ICP
3Diagnostic requirements & thresholds
LP opening pressure >25 cm CSF→Raised ICP confirmed (with normal CSF constituents)
Abducens (VI) palsy present→Permitted — false localising sign; does NOT exclude IIH
Any OTHER focal deficit→IIH excluded — investigate for structural cause
Abnormal scan / venous thrombosis→Not IIH — diagnosis is secondary intracranial hypertension
4Protecting vision & management
The main morbidity is vision loss from chronic papilloedema, so serial visual field and acuity monitoring by ophthalmology is essential.
Weight loss — definitive/first-line; even modest loss can be curative.
Acetazolamide — carbonic anhydrase inhibitor; reduces CSF production.
Topiramate — alternative; adds the benefit of appetite suppression/weight loss.
Therapeutic LP — temporising measure to lower pressure and relieve symptoms.
Stop causative drugs — e.g. tetracyclines, retinoids, oral contraceptives.
Surgery for threatened vision — optic nerve sheath fenestration or CSF shunt (VP/LP shunt).
🚩 The overriding risk is permanent vision loss from papilloedema — arrange urgent ophthalmology review with visual field/acuity monitoring. Before diagnosing IIH you MUST exclude cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (MR/CT venography) and other secondary causes of raised ICP. Remember a sixth nerve palsy is a false localising sign of raised pressure, not evidence of a mass.
🎓 IIH = raised ICP + papilloedema + normal imaging + high LP opening pressure with normal CSF, and no other cause. Think young, obese woman of childbearing age. Treat with weight loss + acetazolamide — and above all, protect vision.

The Spetzler-Martin (S-M) grading scale stratifies the surgical (resection) risk of a cerebral arteriovenous malformation (AVM) — an abnormal tangle of vessels with direct arteriovenous shunting and no intervening capillary bed. Three anatomical features are scored and summed to give a grade from I to V (total 1–5): higher grade predicts greater operative morbidity. It is the standard tool for deciding whether an AVM is a good candidate for microsurgery, radiosurgery, embolisation, or conservative management.

1When it is used & what it predicts
AVMs present with haemorrhage (intracerebral or subarachnoid — the main danger), seizures, headache, or focal neurological deficit, and carry roughly a 2–4% annual haemorrhage risk. Once an AVM is characterised on imaging (CT/CTA, MRI, and catheter angiography — the gold standard for vascular architecture), the S-M grade is applied to estimate the risk of surgical resection and guide multidisciplinary treatment planning. It does not estimate rupture risk itself — only operative morbidity.
2The three components (Size + Eloquence + Drainage)
📏SIZE of nidus
<3 cm = 1 · 3–6 cm = 2 · >6 cm = 3
🧠ELOQUENCE of adjacent brain
Non-eloquent = 0 · Eloquent = 1 (sensorimotor, language, visual cortex, thalamus, hypothalamus, internal capsule, brainstem, cerebellar peduncles, deep cerebellar nuclei)
🩸Venous DRAINAGE pattern
Superficial only = 0 · Any deep venous drainage = 1
3Scoring & thresholds
Sum the three components (range 1–5) to obtain the grade. A separate Grade VI is sometimes reserved for lesions judged inoperable.
Grade I–II (1–2 pts)→Low surgical risk — good candidates for microsurgical resection
Grade III (3 pts)→Intermediate risk — individualised, often multimodal management
Grade IV–V (4–5 pts)→High surgical morbidity — often conservative or multimodal (radiosurgery ± embolisation)
4Interpretation & clinical use
The grade weighs rupture risk against treatment risk across a multidisciplinary team.
Microsurgical resection — curative, favoured for accessible low-grade (I–II) lesions.
Stereotactic radiosurgery — for small or deep/eloquent lesions unsuitable for surgery.
Endovascular embolisation — usually an adjunct to reduce nidus/flow before surgery or radiosurgery.
Conservative — for high-grade lesions where treatment risk exceeds natural-history risk.
Randomised evidence informs decisions for unruptured AVMs, where intervention did not clearly outperform medical management.
🚩 Haemorrhage is the main danger and can be fatal or severely disabling. A higher Spetzler-Martin grade means higher surgical morbidity — grade IV–V lesions are frequently managed non-surgically or multimodally. Ruptured AVMs are generally treated; decisions for unruptured AVMs are individualised. The grade estimates operative risk, not rupture risk, and never replaces multidisciplinary judgement.
🎓 Spetzler-Martin = Size + Eloquence + venous Drainage (deep). Grade I–II are operable/low risk; grade IV–V are high risk. Remember: haemorrhage is the key complication and catheter angiography is the gold standard for defining architecture.

The ABCD2 score was designed to estimate the early risk of stroke after a transient ischaemic attack (TIA). The high-yield exam point today is a guideline change: NICE (2019) no longer uses ABCD2 to risk-stratify TIA — every suspected TIA is now treated as high-risk. Know the components for recognition, but do not use the score as a gatekeeper.

1The five components (max 7)
🎂A — Age
≥60 years — 1
🩺B — Blood pressure
≥140/90 mmHg — 1
🧠C — Clinical features
unilateral weakness — 2; speech disturbance without weakness — 1
⏱️D — Duration
≥60 min — 2; 10–59 min — 1
🍬D — Diabetes
present — 1
2Historical bands (what it predicted)
0–3→historically "low" 2-day stroke risk
4–5→moderate
6–7→high
These bands predicted 2-day stroke risk in the original studies but are no longer used to decide urgency.
3What to do now (current NICE)
Any suspected TIA→give aspirin 300 mg immediately (unless contraindicated) and refer for specialist assessment within 24 hours — regardless of ABCD2
On an anticoagulant, or bleeding risk→arrange urgent imaging to exclude haemorrhage before starting aspirin
Crescendo TIA (≥2 in a week) / AF→discuss urgent specialist assessment / admission
Do not use ABCD2 to delay or triage. Stroke / TIA ›
🚩 Do not withhold urgent (within-24h) specialist assessment because the ABCD2 is "low". NICE treats all suspected TIA as high-risk — aspirin 300 mg + specialist review within 24 hours.
🎓 Exam pearl. The examiner’s trap: ABCD2 still appears in questions, but the modern answer is that NICE abandoned it as a triage tool. Manage every suspected TIA the same — aspirin 300 mg and 24-hour specialist review.
RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__MSK & Trauma:
The Kocher criteria are a clinical prediction tool that estimates the probability that a child presenting with an acutely painful, irritable, atraumatic hip has septic arthritis rather than the far more common (and benign) transient synovitis. Four independent predictors are each worth 1 point; the more predictors present, the higher the likelihood of a joint infection that demands urgent surgical treatment.

1WHEN TO USE IT
Apply it to a child with an atraumatic hip who is limping, refusing to weight-bear, or holding the hip flexed/abducted/externally rotated. The whole point is to answer one question: is this a benign self-limiting synovitis, or a joint-destroying infection? Septic arthritis is an orthopaedic emergency — pus under pressure and bacterial enzymes can irreversibly destroy articular cartilage within hours to days and threaten the blood supply to the femoral head (avascular necrosis). The commonest organism is Staphylococcus aureus; consider Kingella kingae in young children and Neisseria gonorrhoeae in adolescents/adults. Typical picture: hot, swollen, exquisitely tender joint, refusal to move or weight-bear, and systemic upset (fever, malaise).
2THE FOUR PREDICTORS (1 point each)
🚶NON-WEIGHT-BEARING
Unable to bear weight on the affected side
🌡️FEVER
Temperature > 38.5°C
🩸ESR
ESR > 40 mm/hr
⚪WCC
White cell count > 12 × 10&sup9;/L
Each positive predictor scores 1 point, giving a total of 0–4.
Many centres add CRP > 20 mg/L as an additional (or alternative) inflammatory marker — a raised CRP is a strong independent predictor.
3SCORING & PROBABILITY OF SEPTIC ARTHRITIS
0 predictors→Very low risk (< 0.2–2%) — likely transient synovitis
1 predictor→Low risk (~3%)
2 predictors→Intermediate risk (~40%) — low threshold to aspirate
3 predictors→High risk (~93%) — aspiration/washout
4 predictors→Very high risk (~99%) — urgent surgical management
Rising score → higher likelihood of septic arthritis → urgent orthopaedic referral for joint aspiration and washout.
3–4 predictors mandate treating as septic arthritis until proven otherwise.
4INVESTIGATION, MANAGEMENT & LIMITATIONS
Bloods: FBC, CRP, ESR and blood cultures (before antibiotics where possible).
Imaging: ultrasound to detect a joint effusion; X-ray to exclude other pathology (may be normal early).
Definitive test: joint aspiration — Gram stain, culture and synovial WCC; frank pus or organisms confirm the diagnosis.
Management: urgent surgical washout/drainage plus IV antibiotics — do NOT delay treatment.
Differentials: transient synovitis (well child, post-viral, self-limiting), Perthes, SUFE, osteomyelitis, JIA and reactive arthritis.
🚩 Septic arthritis is a surgical emergency — joint aspiration is the definitive test. Even a low Kocher score does NOT fully exclude septic arthritis if clinical suspicion is high, so let the child, not just the number, drive the decision. Delayed treatment leads to irreversible joint destruction and avascular necrosis. Always consider co-existing or masquerading osteomyelitis.
🎓 Four predictors — non-weight-bearing, fever > 38.5°C, ESR > 40, WCC > 12 (many add CRP > 20). 3–4 predictors = high probability (~93–99%) → aspirate/washout. Remember: aspiration is definitive.

The Beighton score is a quick, 9-point clinical screening tool for generalised joint hypermobility (GJH). It assesses whether joints move beyond the normal expected range across five manoeuvres. It is a screen, not a diagnosis: it forms one component of the assessment for hypermobility spectrum disorders (HSD) and hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hEDS), and helps flag patients who may need further evaluation for heritable connective tissue disease.

1When to use it & what it measures
Use the Beighton score when a patient presents with joint pain, recurrent subluxations/dislocations, or features suggesting a connective tissue disorder (soft/stretchy skin, easy bruising, chronic widespread pain, fatigue). It quantifies generalised hypermobility (as opposed to a single lax joint). It is the entry point to the 2017 international hEDS criteria and is used alongside history, systemic features, and family history — a number on its own does not diagnose anything.
2The five manoeuvres (score /9)
🤙5th finger dorsiflexion
Passive dorsiflexion of the little finger beyond 90° — 1 point each side (max 2)
👍Thumb to forearm
Passive apposition of the thumb to the flexor (volar) forearm — 1 point each side (max 2)
💪Elbow hyperextension
Elbow hyperextends beyond 10° — 1 point each side (max 2)
🦵Knee hyperextension
Knee hyperextends beyond 10° — 1 point each side (max 2)
🙇Palms to floor
Forward trunk flexion with knees straight, placing palms flat on the floor — 1 point (midline, non-bilateral)
Four manoeuvres are bilateral (2 points each) and one (palms to floor) is a single midline point — giving a maximum of 9.
Each positive finding scores 1 point; the total is out of 9.
3Scoring & thresholds
Cut-offs are age-dependent and thresholds vary between sources:
≥5 (adults)→Suggests generalised joint hypermobility
≥6 (children/adolescents, pre-pubertal)→Higher threshold as joints are naturally more lax
≥4 (adults over 50)→Lower threshold as flexibility declines with age
Below threshold but symptomatic→Consider historical hypermobility / 5-part questionnaire; may still be HSD
4Interpretation, associations & management
A high score confirms generalised hypermobility, not disease — many people are hypermobile and asymptomatic. When symptomatic, associations include joint pain/instability/dislocations, soft/stretchy skin, easy bruising, chronic widespread pain, fatigue, autonomic dysfunction (e.g. POTS), and GI dysmotility. A diagnosis of hEDS requires the full 2017 international criteria, which combine the Beighton score with systemic features and family history and require exclusion of other EDS types. Management is largely conservative: physiotherapy, targeted muscle strengthening/proprioception, activity pacing, and analgesia, with specialist input for complications.
🚩 The Beighton score is a screen, not a diagnosis — hEDS requires the full 2017 criteria. Always consider and exclude more serious heritable connective tissue disorders: vascular EDS (COL3A1 — arterial and hollow-organ rupture) and Marfan syndrome (aortic root dilatation). These carry vascular/aortic risk and need genetics and cardiology assessment. A high score alone is not pathological.
🎓 Beighton /9 — pinkie, thumb, elbow, knee (×2 each) + palms to floor. ≥5 suggests generalised joint hypermobility in adults; hEDS is diagnosed with the 2017 criteria, not the Beighton score alone.

The revised Ghent nosology (Ghent-2) is the diagnostic framework for Marfan syndrome, an autosomal dominant connective-tissue disorder caused by FBN1 (fibrillin-1) mutations that disrupt TGF-β signalling. It deliberately gives greatest weight to the two cardinal features — aortic root dilatation/aneurysm (or dissection) and ectopia lentis (lens dislocation) — supported by the FBN1 genotype and a weighted systemic features score. It exists to separate true Marfan from its mimics and to trigger the surveillance that prevents fatal aortic dissection.

1WHEN TO USE IT & WHAT IT DIAGNOSES
Apply Ghent-2 to any patient with features suggesting Marfan — tall/arachnodactylic habitus, unexplained aortic root dilatation, ectopia lentis, or a positive family history. It is a diagnostic (not risk-scoring) tool that confirms or excludes Marfan by combining the two cardinal features with genotype and systemic burden. The stakes are high: the diagnosis mandates lifelong cardiac surveillance because aortic root aneurysm and dissection are the leading cause of death.
2THE FOUR DIAGNOSTIC PILLARS
Diagnosis is built from four elements — the two cardinal features carry the most weight.
🫀AORTIC ROOT DILATATION
Cardinal feature. Aortic root Z-score ≥2 (age/BSA-adjusted), aneurysm or dissection
👁️ECTOPIA LENTIS
Cardinal feature. Dislocation of the lens (classically upward/temporal)
🧬FBN1 MUTATION
Causative fibrillin-1 mutation; a mutation known to cause aortic disease carries extra weight
📊SYSTEMIC SCORE
Weighted skeletal/ocular/other features; total ≥7 is contributory
3SYSTEMIC FEATURES SCORE (each weighted; total ≥7 counts)
A tally of body-wide connective-tissue signs; the highest-weighted items are the hand signs, pectus carinatum and facies.
✋WRIST & THUMB SIGN
Both = 3 pts; either one alone = 1 pt
🫁PECTUS
Carinatum = 2 pts; excavatum or chest asymmetry = 1 pt
🧑FACIAL FEATURES
3 of 5 (dolichocephaly, enophthalmos, downslanting fissures, malar hypoplasia, retrognathia) = 1 pt
🦶FOOT & SPINE
Hindfoot deformity (2)/pes planus (1); scoliosis or thoracolumbar kyphosis (1); reduced elbow extension (1)
📏PROPORTIONS
Reduced upper/lower segment ratio + increased arm-span & no severe scoliosis (1)
🩻DURAL & HIP
Dural ectasia (2); protrusio acetabuli (2)
💨PNEUMOTHORAX
Spontaneous pneumothorax (2)
👓EYE / SKIN / VALVE
Myopia >3 dioptres (1); skin striae (1); mitral valve prolapse (1)
4DIAGNOSTIC COMBINATIONS & THRESHOLDS
In the absence of family history, any one of these confirms Marfan:
Aortic root (Z ≥2) + ectopia lentis→Marfan syndrome (two cardinal features)
Aortic root (Z ≥2) + FBN1 mutation→Marfan syndrome
Aortic root (Z ≥2) + systemic score ≥7→Marfan syndrome (exclude mimics first)
Ectopia lentis + FBN1 linked to aortic disease→Marfan syndrome
Positive family history + (ectopia lentis OR score ≥7 OR aortic root Z-threshold)→Marfan syndrome (age-adjusted aortic Z: ≥3 if <20 yrs, ≥2 if ≥20 yrs)
Ectopia lentis + FBN1 not known to cause aortic disease → label as ectopia lentis syndrome, not Marfan.
Systemic score ≥7 or aortic root without a cardinal partner → consider MASS phenotype or MVP syndrome and keep under review.
🚩 The aorta is the killer. Aortic root dilatation and dissection are the life-threatening features and the main cause of death. Every confirmed patient needs regular surveillance echocardiography, a beta-blocker (or losartan/ARB) to slow root growth, and elective prophylactic aortic root replacement at threshold (~5 cm, earlier with family history of dissection or rapid growth). Acute aortic dissection is a surgical emergency (tearing chest/back pain, pulse deficit). Advise against contact and isometric sports; refer to genetics and cardiology. Always exclude homocystinuria — a key mimic — especially if the lens dislocates downward or there is thrombosis/learning difficulty.
🎓 Ghent-2 in one line: aortic root dilatation + ectopia lentis (the two cardinal features) ± FBN1 ± systemic score ≥7. Marfan is autosomal dominant (fibrillin-1, TGF-β). Differentials: Loeys-Dietz, homocystinuria, MASS phenotype, ectopia lentis syndrome. Whatever the route to diagnosis — protect the aorta: echo surveillance, beta-blockers, timely root surgery.

The Ottawa Ankle, Foot & Knee Rules are validated clinical decision rules that tell you when a patient with an acute ankle, foot or knee injury actually needs an X-ray. Applied at the bedside, they safely rule OUT clinically significant fractures with near-100% sensitivity, allowing clinicians to skip imaging in a large proportion of low-risk patients and cut unnecessary radiographs, waiting times and radiation exposure — without missing the fractures that matter.

1WHEN TO USE & WHAT THEY DO
Use in the acute setting after a blunt ankle/foot or knee injury to decide whether radiographs are needed.
They are highly sensitive (approaching 100%) for clinically significant fractures — a NEGATIVE rule reliably excludes fracture, so imaging can be safely withheld.
They are a rule-out tool, not a rule-in tool: a POSITIVE rule identifies who needs an X-ray, not who has a fracture (low specificity).
Rule NEGATIVE→Fracture effectively excluded — X-ray can be safely avoided
Rule POSITIVE→X-ray indicated (does NOT confirm a fracture is present)
2THE CRITERIA — ANKLE vs FOOT vs KNEE
🦶ANKLE — lateral malleolus
Bony tenderness at posterior edge/tip of LATERAL malleolus (distal 6 cm)
🦶ANKLE — medial malleolus
Bony tenderness at posterior edge/tip of MEDIAL malleolus (distal 6 cm)
🚶ANKLE — weight-bear
Unable to bear weight (4 steps) both immediately AND in the ED
🦴FOOT — 5th metatarsal
Bony tenderness at the BASE of the 5TH METATARSAL
🦴FOOT — navicular
Bony tenderness at the NAVICULAR
🚶FOOT — weight-bear
Unable to bear weight (4 steps) immediately AND in the ED
🎂KNEE — age ≥55
Patient aged 55 years or older
🦵KNEE — patella
ISOLATED tenderness of the patella (no other bony tenderness)
🦴KNEE — fibular head
Tenderness at the HEAD of the FIBULA
📐KNEE — flexion
Inability to flex the knee to 90°
🚶KNEE — weight-bear
Unable to bear weight (4 steps) both immediately AND in the ED
3APPLYING THE RULES → IMAGING
Pain in MALLEOLAR zone + malleolar bony tenderness OR can't weight-bear→ANKLE X-ray required (Ottawa Ankle Rules)
Pain in MIDFOOT zone + 5th MT base / navicular tenderness OR can't weight-bear→FOOT X-ray required (Ottawa Foot Rules)
Age ≥55, patella / fibular-head tenderness, can't flex 90°, OR can't weight-bear→KNEE X-ray required (Ottawa Knee Rules)
None of the relevant criteria met→No X-ray needed — reassure, advise, safety-net
4INTERPRETATION, PURPOSE & LIMITATIONS
Purpose: reduce unnecessary radiographs (studies show ~30% fewer ankle/foot films) while maintaining near-100% sensitivity so significant fractures are not missed.
The rules are designed for isolated, cooperative, reliable patients examined for the first time after acute injury.
Reliability is reduced and clinical judgement should override the rule when there is: intoxication, altered mental state, diminished leg sensation (e.g. neuropathy), gross swelling obscuring landmarks, or other distracting/multiple injuries.
They are less well validated in children (commonly cited as unreliable below ~5 years, with ongoing debate up the paediatric age range) and in pregnancy or delayed presentations (>10 days).
🚩 These rules apply only to isolated, cooperative, reliable patients — use caution and clinical judgement in intoxication, altered sensation, gross swelling, or multiple/distracting injuries, and in children. They identify who NEEDS imaging (high sensitivity, low specificity): a POSITIVE rule does NOT mean a fracture is present, and the rules never replace clinical judgement.
🎓 Quick recall — Ankle X-ray = malleolar-zone pain + malleolar bony tenderness OR can't weight-bear; Foot X-ray = midfoot-zone pain + 5th-MT-base/navicular tenderness OR can't weight-bear; Knee X-ray = age ≥55, patella/fibular-head tenderness, can't flex to 90°, or can't weight-bear (4 steps, then & now).

Gurd's criteria (Gurd & Wilson) are the classic clinical diagnostic criteria for fat embolism syndrome (FES) — a systemic disorder caused by fat globules entering the circulation, most often 24–72 hours after a long-bone (femur/tibia) or pelvic fracture (also orthopaedic surgery and intramedullary nailing). FES has no single confirmatory test, so diagnosis is clinical and by exclusion: Gurd requires at least 1 major + 4 minor criteria. The classic triad is respiratory distress, neurological signs, and a petechial rash.

1WHEN TO SUSPECT IT
Think FES in a trauma patient who deteriorates 24–72 hours after a long-bone or pelvic fracture (classically the young patient with a closed femoral shaft fracture), or after intramedullary nailing / orthopaedic surgery. Mechanism is dual: mechanical occlusion of small vessels by fat globules, plus biochemical injury as free fatty acids are released and damage the pulmonary capillary endothelium (an ARDS-like picture). The syndrome is largely subclinical in most fractures but becomes overt in a minority.
2THE CRITERIA — MAJOR vs MINOR

Diagnosis needs at least one MAJOR feature plus four MINOR features. The three major criteria map onto the classic triad.

🫁MAJOR · Respiratory
Respiratory insufficiency / hypoxaemia (tachypnoea, dyspnoea, ARDS-like)
🧠MAJOR · Cerebral
Cerebral involvement — confusion, drowsiness, neuro signs unrelated to head injury
🔴MAJOR · Petechiae
Petechial rash — hallmark; trunk / axilla / conjunctiva (subconjunctival)
🌡️MINOR · Pyrexia
Fever >38.5°C
💓MINOR · Tachycardia
Heart rate >120 bpm
👁️MINOR · Retinal
Retinal changes — fat / petechiae (Purtscher retinopathy)
🟡MINOR · Jaundice
Icterus / hepatic involvement
💧MINOR · Renal
Renal changes — oliguria / anuria, fat in urine
🩸MINOR · Thrombocytopenia
Falling platelet count
🔻MINOR · Anaemia
Falling haemoglobin
📈MINOR · Raised ESR
Elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate
🔬MINOR · Fat globules
Fat macroglobulinaemia — fat in sputum / urine
3MAKING THE DIAGNOSIS
≥1 MAJOR + ≥4 MINOR→Fat embolism syndrome diagnosed (Gurd & Wilson)
Onset 24–72h post fracture→Typical latent window after long-bone / pelvic injury
Petechiae + hypoxia + confusion→Classic triad — strongly suggests FES
The criteria are clinical: there is no gold-standard confirmatory test, so FES remains a diagnosis of exclusion (rule out sepsis, PE, head injury, hypovolaemia).
Petechiae are the most specific sign but appear in only a minority and are transient — look at the conjunctiva, axilla and upper trunk.
4MANAGEMENT & PROGNOSIS

Treatment is largely supportive — there is no specific therapy.

Supportive: oxygen and ventilatory support (may need CPAP/mechanical ventilation), careful fluid balance, and ICU-level care.
Prevention is key: early fracture fixation / immobilisation and careful operative technique reduce incidence.
Prognosis is usually good with supportive care; most cases resolve, though severe respiratory or cerebral disease carries risk.
🚩 Fat embolism syndrome typically presents 24–72h after a long-bone or pelvic fracture with the triad of respiratory distress, neurological signs and a petechial rash. It is a diagnosis of exclusion needing supportive ICU care; prevention is via early fracture fixation. Petechiae — especially conjunctival and axillary — are a key clue and are easily missed.
🎓 Classic triad — hypoxia, confusion, petechial rash; onset 24–72h post long-bone fracture; Gurd = 1 major + 4 minor; management is supportive + early fixation.
RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__Dermatology & Ob:
SCORTEN is a validated severity-of-illness score for Stevens-Johnson Syndrome and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (SJS/TEN). It uses seven simple bedside and laboratory variables, each worth one point, to predict in-hospital mortality and to guide early referral to an ICU or burns unit.

1WHEN TO USE IT & WHAT IT ESTIMATES

Apply SCORTEN to any patient with confirmed or suspected SJS/TEN. It is ideally calculated within the first 24 hours of admission and repeated at 72 hours, as the score often rises early and the day-3 value tracks mortality more accurately. Each of the seven independent risk factors scores one point, giving a total of 0–7, which maps directly onto a predicted probability of death.

Estimates in-hospital mortality in SJS/TEN.
Best measured at 24h and again at 72h.
Guides ICU / burns-unit referral and family counselling.
2THE SEVEN VARIABLES (1 POINT EACH)
🎂AGE
Age ≥ 40 years = 1 point
🦠MALIGNANCY
Associated cancer = 1 point
🫀HEART RATE
HR ≥ 120 bpm = 1 point
🔥SKIN DETACHMENT
Epidermal detachment / BSA > 10% = 1 point
💧SERUM UREA
Urea > 10 mmol/L = 1 point
🧪BICARBONATE
HCO₃⁻ < 20 mmol/L = 1 point
🍬GLUCOSE
Glucose > 14 mmol/L = 1 point
3SCORING & MORTALITY BANDS

Add the points and read off the predicted in-hospital mortality. Higher scores warrant intensive supportive care in a specialist setting.

0–1 points→~3% mortality
2 points→~12% mortality
3 points→~35% mortality
4 points→~58% mortality
≥ 5 points→~90% mortality
4INTERPRETATION & LIMITATIONS

SCORTEN provides objective prognostic information that supports the decision to transfer to an ICU or burns unit and helps frame realistic conversations with patients and families. It performs best when calculated within the first 72 hours; used outside that window or at the extremes of severity it can underestimate the true risk, particularly in the sickest patients with rapidly progressive detachment.

🚩 SCORTEN supports but does not replace clinical judgement. A low score in a deteriorating patient still mandates escalation, and the score can underestimate mortality at extremes of illness or when calculated late.
🎓 High-yield: seven variables, one point each. Remember that skin detachment is the only dermatological variable — the other six are age, malignancy, tachycardia, and three metabolic labs (urea, bicarbonate, glucose).

The LRINEC score (Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotising Fasciitis) is a bedside tool that uses six routine blood tests to stratify the risk that a soft-tissue infection is necrotising fasciitis rather than severe cellulitis or abscess. It converts cheap, widely available bloods into a single 0–13 score, flagging patients who warrant urgent surgical review. It is an adjunct that raises suspicion — it does not confirm or exclude the diagnosis.

1When to use it & what it estimates

Apply LRINEC when a patient presents with a soft-tissue infection and you need to gauge how likely necrotising fasciitis is. Classic red flags — pain out of proportion to skin findings, rapid spread, systemic toxicity, crepitus, skin bullae or necrosis — should already prompt concern; LRINEC adds a laboratory dimension to support (not replace) that clinical judgement.

Distinguishes necrotising fasciitis from severe cellulitis using deranged inflammatory and metabolic bloods.
Best value is a HIGH score in an equivocal case — it escalates urgency toward surgical exploration.
2The six laboratory variables
🔥CRP
≥150 mg/L → 4 points (the single heaviest variable)
⚪White cell count
15–25 ×10&sup9;/L → 1 point; >25 → 2 points
🩸Haemoglobin
11–13.5 g/dL → 1 point; <11 → 2 points
🧂Sodium
<135 mmol/L → 2 points (hyponatraemia)
🧪Creatinine
>141 µmol/L → 2 points
🍬Glucose
>10 mmol/L → 1 point

Adding every maximum gives a maximum score of 13 (CRP 4 + WBC 2 + Hb 2 + Na 2 + creatinine 2 + glucose 1).

3Scoring & risk bands
≤5→Low risk — <50% probability of necrotising fasciitis
6–7→Intermediate risk — observe closely, low threshold to escalate
≥8→High risk — >75% probability; urgent surgical involvement
4Interpretation & limitations

LRINEC was derived retrospectively and later validation studies show variable, often modest sensitivity. A meaningful proportion of biopsy-proven cases score in the low band, so a reassuring score in a toxic patient is dangerous reassurance. Treat a raised score as a strong prompt to act and a low score as non-contributory when clinical suspicion is high.

🚩 Necrotising fasciitis is a SURGICAL diagnosis made at operative exploration. A LOW LRINEC does NOT exclude it and must NEVER delay urgent surgical exploration and debridement when clinical suspicion is high. Broad-spectrum antibiotics and resuscitation run in parallel — the score never overrides the clinical picture.
🎓 CRP ≥150 mg/L alone contributes 4 of the 13 points, more than any other variable — a common exam favourite. Remember the safety headline: LRINEC supports the decision to operate, it never withholds it.

The Eron classification (from the CREST guidelines, echoed in UK/NICE cellulitis guidance) stratifies cellulitis and other skin & soft-tissue infections into four classes (I–IV). It is not a points-based score but a clinical severity grade that answers two practical questions: does this patient need admission, and do they need oral or intravenous antibiotics? Class rises with systemic toxicity and with comorbidities that threaten the limb or slow healing.

1When to use it
Apply at the point of assessing any adult with cellulitis or erysipelas to decide the route of care. It is used alongside the presence of systemic sepsis features and comorbidities to triage between community oral treatment, OPAT (outpatient parenteral antibiotic therapy) / short admission, and urgent inpatient management. NICE recommends admitting or referring people with Eron Class III or IV, and considering referral for Class II where oral community care is not feasible.
2The four classes
🟢CLASS I
No signs of systemic toxicity and no uncontrolled comorbidity
🟡CLASS II
Systemically unwell, OR systemically well but with a comorbidity (peripheral vascular disease, chronic venous insufficiency, morbid obesity) that may complicate or slow resolution
🟠CLASS III
Significant systemic upset (acute confusion, tachycardia, tachypnoea, hypotension) OR unstable comorbidities that may interfere with response, or a limb-threatening infection
🔴CLASS IV
Sepsis or a severe, life-threatening infection such as necrotising fasciitis
3Class → management
Class I→Community management with oral antibiotics (e.g. flucloxacillin); safety-net and review
Class II→Short-term admission or OPAT / IV antibiotics; treat comorbidity that slows resolution
Class III→Admit for IV antibiotics and monitoring; stabilise unstable comorbidity / limb-threatening infection
Class IV→Urgent inpatient admission, sepsis management and immediate surgical assessment (necrotising infection)
4Interpretation & limitations
The class is dynamic — re-grade if the patient deteriorates or fails to improve within 48 hours of oral therapy.
Comorbidity alone (e.g. chronic venous insufficiency, morbid obesity) can lift an otherwise well patient into Class II even without systemic upset.
Eron grades severity but does not identify the organism or the need for surgery; combine with sepsis screening and clinical judgement.
🚩 Class III–IV disease, or cellulitis that is rapidly spreading, has pain disproportionate to skin findings, crepitus, skin necrosis, bullae or a systemically septic patient, warrants urgent assessment for necrotising fasciitis and emergency admission — do not wait to see if oral antibiotics work.
🎓 High-yield: NICE/CREST say admit (or refer for consideration of admission) anyone who is Eron Class III or IV. Remember Class II can be systemically well with a complicating comorbidity OR systemically unwell — both routes qualify.

The Weighted 7-Point Checklist is a scoring aide-mémoire recommended by NICE to help identify pigmented skin lesions that need urgent assessment for possible melanoma. It splits seven clinical features into three major features (worth 2 points each) and four minor features (worth 1 point each); a total of 3 or more flags a lesion as suspicious and prompts an urgent suspected-cancer (2-week-wait) referral to dermatology.

1When to use it
Apply the checklist in primary care to any new or changing pigmented skin lesion the patient or clinician is worried about. It is a triage tool to decide who needs urgent specialist review, not a diagnostic test — the weighting reflects that changes in size, shape and colour carry the most malignant significance.
2The seven features and their points
📏Change in size
MAJOR — 2 points
🔷Irregular shape/border
MAJOR — 2 points
🎨Irregular colour
MAJOR — 2 points
📐Diameter ≥7 mm
MINOR — 1 point (largest diameter)
🔥Inflammation
MINOR — 1 point
💧Oozing/crusting
MINOR — 1 point
🌡️Change in sensation
MINOR — 1 point (itch/altered sensation)
3Scoring and the referral threshold
Add 2 points for each major feature present and 1 point for each minor feature present (maximum 10).
The three major features alone are the highest-yield discriminators of melanoma.
Score ≥3→Suspicious — urgent suspected-cancer (2-week-wait) referral to dermatology
Score <3→Lower suspicion — consider review/monitoring, but refer if any single feature is strongly suspicious
4Contrast with the ABCDE rule
The other widely used melanoma aide-mémoire is ABCDE: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Colour variation, Diameter >6 mm, and Evolution (change over time). ABCDE is an unweighted checklist that is quick for patient self-examination and public health messaging, whereas the 7-point checklist assigns weighted points and a numerical threshold to structure a referral decision. Both point at the same core danger signs — change, irregular border and irregular colour.
🚩 Refer any lesion that is strongly suspicious of melanoma even if the total score is below 3 — a single worrying feature (e.g. a growing, ulcerating or bleeding pigmented lesion) overrides the number. The checklist is a triage aid only and does not replace dermoscopy and specialist assessment, which remain necessary to confirm or exclude melanoma.
🎓 Remember the weighting: the three major features (change in size, irregular shape, irregular colour) score 2 each, so any two major features alone reach the 2-week-wait threshold of 3+ once combined with a single minor feature — or two majors give 4 outright.

The PUQE score (Pregnancy-Unique Quantification of Emesis) is a simple, validated tool that grades the severity of nausea and vomiting of pregnancy (NVP) and hyperemesis gravidarum. It captures symptoms over the previous 24 hours using three questions, each scored 1–5, giving a total of 3–15. RCOG Green-top Guideline 69 recommends it to objectively assess NVP severity and guide management and escalation.

1When to use it & what it measures
Use PUQE in any pregnant woman presenting with nausea and/or vomiting to quantify severity and track response to treatment. It is a severity score, not a diagnostic test — it does not by itself confirm hyperemesis gravidarum. Interpret it alongside markers of dehydration, ketonuria, weight loss and the ability to tolerate oral fluids.
2The three components (each 1–5, previous 24 h)
🤢Hours of nausea
Total hours feeling nauseated: none (1) → more than 6 h (5)
🥂Vomiting episodes
Number of times actually vomited: none (1) → 7 or more (5)
😫Retching episodes
Number of dry heaves / retching without bringing anything up: none (1) → 7 or more (5)
Add the three answers together for a total from 3 (minimum, symptom-free) to 15 (maximum).
A PUQE-24 variant covers the full previous 24 hours and is the version used in UK guidance.
3Scoring bands & management ladder
≤ 6→Mild NVP — manage in the community with oral antiemetics and lifestyle/dietary advice
7–12→Moderate NVP — oral/regular antiemetics; consider ambulatory or day-case IV fluids if not tolerating intake
≥ 13→Severe NVP — consider admission for IV rehydration and IV antiemetics
Escalate regardless of score when the woman cannot keep down oral fluids or oral antiemetics, or has significant ketonuria, weight loss or dehydration.
4Interpretation & clinical use
Repeating PUQE lets you track response objectively — a falling score after antiemetics and rehydration confirms improvement, while a persistently high score supports admission or a change of therapy. It is quick, reproducible and correlates with quality of life and need for hospital care, making it ideal for both first assessment and follow-up.
🚩 PUQE guides but does not replace assessment of dehydration, ketosis and electrolytes — always check weight, urinary ketones, U&Es and fluid tolerance. In prolonged or severe vomiting give thiamine to prevent Wernicke’s encephalopathy.
🎓 Remember the three bands as 6 / 12 / 13: ≤6 mild, 7–12 moderate, ≥13 severe. The minimum possible score is 3, not 0, because each item scores at least 1.
